member of the commission . – (de) honoured president, esteemed representative of the council presidency, ladies and gentlemen, it is inappropriate that the representative for the acting commission should make a full statement on the finnish presidency"s programme here, for this programme will largely be implemented under the new commission. permit me, therefore, to restrict my comments in the main to two issues, namely reconstruction in kosovo and the sentence passed on abdullah öçalan. firstly, i should like to remind you that from the very beginning, the european union was heavily involved in the endeavours being made to bring about a peaceful resolution of the kosovo conflict. the commission also provided humanitarian aid throughout the conflict. the european union is, as we are all aware, the largest donor. we gave financial aid to those countries most severely affected by the influx of exiles and refugees. now that the conflict is over, our immediate priority is to support kfor"s endeavours to restore peace and order and to reconstruct a functioning civil administration under the leadership of the united nations. the european union has a special task to fulfil in this respect. in particular, we bear the responsibility for the reconstruction aspects of unmig. jollie dixon, the acting special delegate for the commission appointed for this purpose, has now taken up his position in pristina and it is time to solve the huge number of practical problems. what has been provided so far in terms of aid? the humanitarian aid committed to kosovo and the neighbouring countries totals eur 378 million, with the bulk going towards providing essential foods and other goods such as medicines, sanitation equipment and accommodation. this aid is channelled through the unhcr, the international red cross, unicef and various ngos. this amount includes the eur 196 million currently being mobilised from the commission"s budgetary reserves. furthermore, eur 100 million were committed as macroeconomic aid for the damage sustained by other countries as a result of the kosovo crisis, 62 million being earmarked for albania, 25 million for fyrom and 13 million for montenegro. the first instalments have already been paid out. in addition, eur 45 million will be committed to kosovo through the obnova programme, a first priority of which will be to finance a delegation whose task is to ascertain the scale of material damage. the first set of findings will be available on 23 july. the european commission will then base its definitive aid programme on these figures. in addition, the budgetary requirements for reconstruction will need to be set in the course of the next two to three years, and the anticipated costs which the other donors are to incur will need to be calculated. the measures to be financed under the obnova programme as a matter of priority include such areas as mine clearance, obtaining materials for rebuilding houses and also public buildings, supporting public utilities and customs control, and a village employment and rehabilitation programme. working in conjunction with kfor, unmig and unhcr, these projects were prioritised and they are to supplement the on-going work undertaken by the humanitarian organisations. we hope to be able to commit the eur 45 million before the end of this month. as explained to the budgetary authorities in the trialogue of 2 july, an additional eur 92 million will still be required this year. it was agreed during this trialogue session that in september the commission will submit a proposal to increase the budget by means of an amending and supplementary budget which will raise the 92 million required. the funds are largely to be raised by reallocation, with as little utilisation as possible being made of additional funds. it was also agreed that both parts of the budgetary authorities will deal with this proposal in one reading. we are counting on receiving parliament"s support as far as this is concerned, so that the european community can continue to play a leading role in the reconstruction process. i should now like to say a few words on the issue of a reconstruction agency. before the cologne european council meeting, the commission proposed to the heads of state and government that a special agency should be set up which would deal with the implementation of the reconstruction work. the european council followed this recommendation and instructed the commission back in june to formulate an actual proposal on the basis of experience gained from bosnia. we at the commission proposed that the agency should be located in pristina, that is at the centre of reconstruction activity, where all the other international organisations are located. (applause) however, at the informal meeting of heads of state and government in rio, the heads of government agreed that the agency ‘s seat should be in thessaloniki. we cannot escape the conclusion though, that this was due not so much to the fact that the reconstruction activities, for which this agency was to be responsible, were in the immediate vicinity, but rather to the fact that there was a general need for economic aid throughout the region. the commission takes the view that it will only be possible to work effectively if the vast proportion of activities is concentrated in pristina. however, the commission could envisage a solution whereby, for example, some of the administrative personnel would be based at another location. but this must not be to the detriment of the efficiency and effectiveness of the operation. the commission assumes that to uphold these principles accords with the court of auditors" position and the first reactions of the european parliament. however, the council decided conclusively on monday this week that the agency"s seat should be in thessaloniki. the commission has refrained from stating its position, preferring the commission"s definitive position to be established by the new commission. the proposal has now been submitted to parliament for advice. meanwhile, as of 1 july, the commission has been despatching a task force consisting of approximately 20 officials and supporting personnel to pristina, where it will be responsible for implementing the reconstruction programme. all authority required to effect implementation was transferred from brussels to the leader of the task force in pristina in order to create a mechanism which will work with optimum efficiency and speed to provide aid at a time when it is most urgently needed in kosovo. finally, a comment on achieving co-ordination amongst the donors. on 13 july, a meeting took place of the high level steering group, the committee managed by the european commission and the world bank which is based on partnership and is intended to co-ordinate the kosovo crisis aid provided by international donors. it was confirmed on this occasion that the first kosovo donor conference would be held on 28 july in brussels. this conference is to focus in particular on determining what the pressing needs will be from now until the end of the year. a second donor conference has been planned for october and this will deal in greater depth with the reconstruction efforts. turning to the öçalan trial, the commission takes the same position on this matter as that taken up by the german presidency on 29 june, following the death sentence passed by the state security tribunal of ankara on abdullah öçalan, and again expresses its absolute repudiation of the death penalty. it was for this reason that on 29 june, the commission asked the relevant turkish authorities to take account of the european union"s repudiation of this death penalty. consequently, the commission, knowing that turkey has not employed the death penalty since 1984, anticipates that as a member of the council of europe, turkey will abide by the obligations that it has entered into. to carry out the death penalty would inevitably place relations between the european union and turkey under huge strain. like the majority of eu member states, the commission believes that recent amendments to turkish legislation have paved the way for the case against mr öçalan and the process of reaching a verdict, to be transferred to a civil court. - mr president, kosovo is a small economy. the european union could subsidise kosovo for ever and hardly notice it. but surely this is not an acceptable solution. as soon as possible, we must aim to have kosovo stand on its own economic feet. that inevitably means external trade. however, there is a problem in redeveloping kosovo's trade. its biggest trading partner in the past and almost certainly in the future must be its neighbour immediately to the north, serbia proper. not only that but its trade routes to much of the rest of europe past through serbia. and yet serbia is a pariah, embargoed, its infrastructure largely destroyed, its economy shattered. here we have a conundrum: how do we get kosovo to stand on its own feet unless we can rehabilitate serbia also? the current international community's set purpose is that milosevic and his regime must be got rid of and then everything is possible. until he goes, not a penny – well, we heard earlier, hardly a penny. but what if milosevic does not go? let us hope that he does, but if he does not, have we begun to estimate the cost of restoring serbia's infrastructure and productive economy? remember, serbia was a sizeable, developed industrial economy, a vital trading partner and transport corridor for bulgaria, romania, turkey, greece, as well as kosovo and all the former yugoslav republics. so my question to the president-in-office of the council and to the commission is this: how far have you thought through the political steps, the economic and financial commitments that are needed to bring about a free and democratic serbia and reintegrate a free and democratic serbia into the european economy and body politic?

council . - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, right at the start, i would also like to congratulate you on your election to this parliament. i wish you all every success in the discharge of your demanding duties. as a representative of the country that now holds the presidency, i shall be personally present at the part-session in september. i really appreciate having the opportunity to work together with you all. in a letter from him dated 9 june, mr bangemann, then member of the commission, informed the then president of the commission, gerhard schröder, of his intention to enter the service of a private telecommunications company, the spanish firm telefónica . the council immediately looked into the matter, deciding on 9 july to take the case to the european court of justice, on the basis of article 213 (2(3)) of the ec treaty and the regulations contained in the ecsc treaty and the euratom treaty. under the ec treaty, members of the commission must make a solemn declaration, when commencing their duties, that they will honour their obligations of membership, during their term of office and after it has ended, and behave with integrity and discretion, in the acceptance, after their term of office has ended, of certain appointments or benefits. in the view of the council, mr bangemann, who has, since 1992, been the commission member expressly responsible for telecommunications, was in breach of the regulations. the council believes he was under an obligation to decline telefónica"s offer. the court will decide whether the member of the commission was in breach of the ec treaty or not. while handling the bangemann case, the council noticed with satisfaction how swiftly the future president of the commission was to act after the case was brought. it is the common objective of the council, the future president of the commission, romano prodi, and all the candidates for membership of the commission to prevent the repetition in future of similar conflicts of interest, such as that which occurred in the bangemann case. professor prodi, in his own programme of reforms for the commission, has stressed the need for transparency, efficiency and accountability. when he spoke earlier today here in the european parliament, he told us what demands he would be making in practice on the members of the new commission. for example, there will be clear rules for new members regarding what sort of posts would be appropriate for them to take up on departure from the commission. members of the commission must also, if requested, allow an independent ethics committee to investigate any future post up to a year after they have ceased to hold office, to ensure the new job is compatible in its nature with the work of the commission. the council and its president warmly support the rules on behaviour that romano prodi has given notice of, and they are a good start on the road to comprehensive reforms. besides the members of the commission, all others in the service of the institutions of the union must be able to demonstrate that they are adhering to the principle of transparency and complying with commonly accepted rules of behaviour. i am happy to note that the commission has acted in accordance with the wishes of both the council and parliament and begun preparations to alter rules relating to personnel policy. we need precise rules. only credible reforms will bring the commission and the union as a whole closer to the public and increase the confidence of our citizens in the union and its institutions. commission. – can i join mr sasi in congratulating members of the house on the election that they achieved to this parliament and particularly congratulate, as mr sasi did, the new members of the house? i hope that they will find their tasks and their career here are both fascinating and fulfilling in the service of the people who have elected them. the resolution for debate relates to specific events and to principles concerning the conduct of commissioners. i will therefore respond on behalf of the commission by reporting briefly on those events and on the commission's reaction to them. on 29 june 1999, the president of the commission, mr santer was made aware of the decision of mr bangemann to depart from the commission in order to take up a private sector appointment two days later on 1 july 1999. mr santer wrote to mr bangemann on 30 june 1999 informing him that he would be put on functional leave and that his responsibilities would be transferred to a colleague in the commission. in that letter, mr santer stipulated that mr bangemann could not commence his new duties and his new activities until the procedure set out in article 215 of the treaty had been completed and he also said that he would submit to the college the question of the compatibility of that planned appointment with article 213 of the treaty. on 1 july 1999, the commission discussed the matter before beginning its formal scheduled meeting. mr bangemann attended those proceedings and stated that he had not acted and would not act in ways that breached article 213. the commission formally took note of those statements from mr bangemann. the house will be familiar with article 213 which, amongst other things, requires members of the commission in particular ‘to behave with integrity and discretion as regards the acceptance, after they have ceased to hold office, of certain appointments'. all commissioners, mr president, appear before the court of justice to swear an oath to that effect on taking up office. at the meeting held on 1 july 1999, commissioners expressed their views to mr bangemann and he then withdrew from the room. commissioners subsequently considered the issues raised by these events and their conclusions are set out in a statement which was published on 1 july 1999 and extensively reported. on 9 july 1999, as the house will have heard from mr sasi, the council decided to refer this case to the court of justice under article 213 of the treaty and, following that decision, it is now for the court to pronounce on the matters. honourable members will understand that the case is therefore now sub judice and the commission consequently has to abstain from public comment on it. as a general indication of the view of the commission on the issues posed by the motion before the house, i refer honourable members to the concluding paragraph of the commission's statement of 1 july 1999 which expressed the view ‘that it would be advisable for the future to clarify the implementation of article 213 regarding commission members' activities after they have ceased to hold office'. the commission consequently notes that on 17 july 1999 the president and commission-designate agreed upon and published a draft code of conduct for commissioners. as the house will have seen from press reports, that document specifies clear compulsory requirements for future commissioners who intend to engage in any occupation during the year after they leave office to inform the commission of their intentions in good time. it further provides for a procedure of examination and decision-making that includes the specific power of the commission to refer the matter to an ethics committee when a commissioner's planned occupation is related to his or her portfolio. the house may also wish to know that, in the course of discussions this month, members of the existing commission who have always fully respected their solemn undertaking to meet the obligations of integrity and discretion have readily and voluntarily reaffirmed that commitment. to them, as to me of course, it is axiomatic. the house will be aware that the composite version of the resolution for debate before this parliament today was produced this morning in keeping with usual practice. the commission has therefore had no opportunity to discuss the specific call in the motion for resolution for current commissioners to respect voluntarily the new code of conduct. i have, however, consulted the acting president, mr marín, and can inform the house that this issue will receive the attention of the commission at its meeting next week. i have sought to respond to the motion for debate as fully as possible whilst respecting the fact that the case which prompted the question is now sub judice . i know that the house will share my awareness of the fact that this debate and my later response to it will need to take account of that obvious legal consideration.

mr president, given the history of the united kingdom in relation to the bse crisis, some delegates may consider that the uk is disqualified from giving an objective view. however, such a view would be wrong. it must be remembered that this was not our only crisis. we also had salmonella in eggs and listeria, giving us unparalleled experience in dealing with food safety crises. on the matter of listeria, this crisis came to a head in 1989 when over 200 babies and young children had been killed in preceding years, far more than died of new variant cjd. what fellow members may not know is that the main source of the disease was contaminated paté sold from three belgian plants. only when uk health officials intervened was the problem finally resolved. what this says is that it is not just the uk that has food safety problems. but what we have learned from our incidents is that precipitate reaction can often do more damage than the initial crises. action needs to be carefully considered and based on good science. in response to the dioxin incident, we see the commission launching once again into frenzied legislative action. this is damaging british interests, in particular a company called spalding nutrition which is threatened by an entirely unnecessary ban. thus, we would say: by all means have an enquiry, but first let us have a wide-ranging review of all member states' systems for dealing with food and health scares, starting with an evaluation of the british system.
the dioxin story is very familiar to those of us in the united kingdom who have lived through bse. many of the ingredients are exactly the same – disagreeable and even disgusting practices in the preparation of some animal foodstuffs in a world of intensive agriculture and panic and deceit in some of the member states concerned when the source of contamination is first discovered. we must remember this was discovered in january 1999 and the commission was only able to take action after a period of months and a good deal of obfuscation. what we have now seen is the same set of arguments that perhaps they were trying to avoid: a consumer panic and protection of a market – a market which is actually now much more imperilled by the way in which the crisis has unfolded. i think there are dangers of overreaction and some members have referred to that. what i would say is that we must learn lessons from this crisis. firstly, a vigorous and properly funded inspectorate must be established to take a preventative role in this matter. we are now talking about significant changes in the law, long lists of further regulations of substances which may be banned. i certainly do not know, because i do not have the technical expertise, whether the range of recovered vegetable oils which are now seen to be a source of risk should be subject to an outright ban, or whether it should simply be limited to some section of kitchen waste which should never have been in any form of animal foodstuff in the first instance. what i do know is that the inspectorate which we have fought for – we had to fight to get an effective budget for it, to set up the veterinary office in brussels and to make sure that we had the principle of general inspections throughout the community – that inspectorate finds itself threatened and bullied. we have had examples in my country and in belgium of people being physically threatened, of being blackmailed and in some instances even murdered! now when that is the situation, how can we say that the proposal, welcome as it is, to look at a europe-wide food and drugs agency and all these grand gestures can work when no individual inspector can penetrate into the world of crime and fraud which characterises sections of this industry. so, in my opinion, we have to put our own house in order in this matter. we have to be able to say, as the motion of the socialist group does, that the rule of law must apply, that we are a community of law, and unless we have a universal application, which never happened in the wake of bse, of the regulations, the situation cannot improve. simply to bring forward new lists to imperil the producers and not to safeguard the consumer in the actions involved is the wrong way forward.
mr president, i want to focus on one particular issue which i feel has not been fully explored. dioxin, and in this case its source chemical pcb, is one of the number of non-biodegradable bio-accumulative chemicals that we know are contaminating the food chain around the world. there are rules and regulations already in existence for the correct and proper disposal of these substances. indeed, i was parliament's rapporteur on the council and commission proposal for the elimination of pcbs and pcds we dealt with in the last parliament. we have to ask if these existing european rules and regulations are being properly followed. are the responsible authorities given the duty to dispose of these chemicals in a correct and safe way, following the rules, or are they deliberately avoiding them and disposing of these chemicals in the wrong way? this incident appears to indicate that is the case. unlike bacterial or some other form of organic or biological contamination of the food chain, we have here a finite quantity of substance that could easily be eliminated. would the commission please look into why the regulations on the proper disposal of pcbs and pcds are not being correctly followed? will they please investigate where the substances came from that caused this incident?

commission.- i should like to begin by responding to the words of maij-weggen. the point is well made and well taken. i know that she feels strongly about this and that she is not alone in that. whilst i obviously cannot commit my colleague, mrs loyola de palacio, who is happily a member of this house at the present time, to the development of her policy and approach in this house, there are several who feel that the time is right for further discussion between the commission and parliament on some of the procedures and conventions of this house, which obviously meets in more than one place, as well as the conventions and procedures of the college. i hope that discussion can proceed without great delay because there could be developments which would be of mutual benefit and would actually promote accountability and transparency in the service of the union. on the question before the house, i would like to make the following statement on behalf of the commission. this week, the commission issued a formal legal decision against the local organisers of last year's football world cup tournament in france. the organisers were the cfo. that decision followed the organisation's use of discriminatory sales arrangements for tickets for matches. as the house will recall, in 1996 and 1997 the system used by cfo favoured consumers who were able to provide an address in france. in the view of the commission, that constituted an abuse of the organisation's dominant position in the market which is contrary to article 82 of the treaty. this was the first case in community history in which article 82 of the treaty has been used to penalise a discriminatory practice that harms the interests of consumers without having a significant effect on the market. in reaching its decision therefore, the commission took account of the fact that there were no previous decisions of the commission or case-law from the court of justice to guide cfo in its ticketing policy. in addition it was evident that the ticketing arrangements used by cfo in 1996 and 1997 were exactly similar to those employed in previous world cup tournaments and other similar major international contests. as the house will recall, the commission responded to complaints from people outside france who were finding it impossible to buy tickets by beginning an investigation. the cfo then quickly changed its policy and made efforts to make sure that tickets sold in 1998 were available without discrimination. then 100, 000 tickets became available to everyone on a first-come-first-served basis. the commission judged that these factors – the unprecedented application of the law, the conventions relating to previous ticket sales for international tournaments, and the constructive action of cfo – justified a symbolic rather than a punitive fine. in addition, it is relevant to add that a more substantial fine on the organisers of the 1998 world cup in france would have imposed an obligation on the commission to consider action against the organisers of previous major tournaments who used exactly the same ticketing policies. this could have meant, for example, action against the organisers of the 1996 european championship because on that occasion, supporters benefitted from a sales scheme which favoured nationals over fans from abroad. the french organising committee is not a normal commercial profit-seeking company. it exists for the interests of football and it is important to recognise that all profits reverted to the game of football. fining the french organising committee means taking money away from grassroots football and from the promotion of the game and putting that money into the coffers of the european commission. i do not believe that any genuine lover of football would think that was either sensible or acceptable. i know that football supporters in parts of the union have strongly criticised the size of the eur 1, 000 fine. my colleagues and i can certainly understand such reactions when those reactions are not informed by the facts. i hope, however, that in this house and elsewhere, there will be recognition of the specific factors directly relevant to this case. the important – and i think the instructive – outcome of the case is plain. all future sports tournament organisers now clearly know that any ticketing arrangements must comply fully with european community competition rules and be non-discriminatory. secondly, they know that the commission will not hesitate to take action against any organiser that fails to comply with those rules. thirdly, they know that the symbolic approach could only be followed once, and in very particular circumstances. these realities, in the view of the commission, mean that standards of fair treatment for sports fans have been clarified and strengthened. they will definitely enjoy protection against discrimination in the future. the organisers of the euro−2000 cup in belgium and the netherlands have, for instance, contacted the commission and as a result, they have adapted their sales system to meet the requirements of community law. there has been no previous occasion on which a higher percentage of tickets has been made available to the general public with absolutely equal rights for all citizens of the european union. we intend to keep it that way. that is the silver lining. it is a pity that first there had to be a cloud.

- the next item is the report (a5-0003/99) by mrs mckenna, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council decision establishing a community framework for cooperation in the field of accidental marine pollution.
commission - (es) mr president, i thank the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, and in particular its rapporteur, mrs mckenna, and the members of the committee on budgets for the work they have done and the interest they have shown in this proposal. you will agree with me that this community framework for cooperation is important, as it is intended to support and complement the work of the member states in the field of accidental marine pollution, precisely in order to make it more effective. this framework has already proved to be very useful when, in the face of serious spills, the work of different member states had to be coordinated. the commission can accept in whole or in part 20 of the 29 proposed amendments which clearly improve the proposal. amendments nos 3, 6, 8, 9 and 13 and part of amendment no 15 would be acceptable in principle, although we would like them to be worded differently. the remaining nine amendments pose problems for the following reasons: - amendment no 1 and, in part, amendments nos 5, 15 and 24 introduce a specific reference to pollution caused by radioactive substances, which are already implicitly regulated in the proposal. in addition, the existing international conventions on the protection of the mediterranean sea, the baltic sea and the north sea, to which the community is a contracting party, all follow the same approach: they do not specifically mention any substance; - amendments nos 10, 11, 12, 17 and 18 and the first part of amendment no 22 are aimed at strengthening cooperation with countries participating in the phare, tacis and meda programmes. this inclusion can greatly complicate management, given the differences between the decision-making processes and the proposed community framework; - according to the commission, amendment no 22 is not in line with the recent decision on comitology; - in our view, amendment no 23 infringes the commission's right of initiative. despite these details, i am confident that parliament's input and support will enable this proposal to be adopted quickly in order to ensure continuity between the present community action and the programme proposed to enter into force on 1 january 2000.
the rapporteur. -(en) mr president, i am speaking as rapporteur on the proposal for a european commission recommendation laying down minimum criteria for environmental inspections. the most important thing about my report is that with the support of the committee, i rejected the idea that it should be a recommendation. i want to make sure that this instrument is a directive. i am quite convinced that the speech which mr marin is now reading with anxiety rejects everything i am about to say. this is a very important point and is the source of some of the disappointment felt by citizens in many countries with the european union. it is based on the feeling that legislation adopted at eu level is not uniformly implemented across the member states of the european union. i do not know what my colleagues in the european parliament think, but it was certainly one of the criticisms of the european union during the british campaign leading up to the european parliament elections. at present, more than 80 infringement cases against environmental legislation in the european union, involving 11 member states, are pending before the court of justice. as rapporteur on the recent discharge directive, i know that the european commission proposes legislation on the assumption that it will be adopted and properly implemented in all member states. at the same time, however, the directorate-general concerned is fully aware that in certain areas and in certain member states there is no inspection service to check the effective application of these laws. the european commission's recipe for dealing with this problem is to organise occasional meetings of inspectors from the different member states to try to improve their techniques and to work this into a recommendation. there is really nothing particularly radical about it. the committee on the environment feels that this is largely inadequate and that without a directive, the member states lagging behind will not be encouraged to do anything. the advantage of changing from a recommendation to a directive is twofold. firstly, the possibility of financial penalties and sanctions is likely to be a catalyst for change and secondly, taking up the draft recommendation before us avoids creating a directive which is too normative and detailed. people want to see the legislation implemented. they don't want paperwork. if this instrument is turned into a directive, it would mean that we could see who in the commission and among the members of this parliament is actually doing something. if we are satisfied with one recommendation, it is likely that in five years' time we may forget to report to parliament that a recommendation has been adopted and that little has been done about it. a directive has the force of law and we think that is what we need. i note that the greens have tabled an amendment calling the attention of the european parliament to the fact that there must be some sort of environmental inspection office at european union level. we must proceed very carefully in this matter if we do not want to entangle the member states in more paperwork. rather than embarking on the establishment of a supranational inspection office, with all the difficulties that this implies in terms of access rights, it is better to ensure, once the legislation is in place, that (a) environmental inspections exist in all member states and (b) that they perform their task to a more or less similar standard. you can only do this through a management. a recommendation is largely inadequate.
- mr president, the european union is the subject of much criticism but few voices are raised to protest when this institution takes action to protect our air, rivers, seas and countryside, because everyone is aware that pollution does not know the borders of nations and can only be effectively combated by countries working together. let's do justice to europe: it has done pioneering work by introducing legislation on environmental protection. but laws that are not uniformly applied by the 15 member states will succumb to the cynicism of those who seek financial gain at any cost and will engender a sense of injustice and, ultimately, hostility among all those who follow the rules. of course, none of us have any reason to feel superior. no country is perfect in enforcing environmental laws. this report is a step forward and gives parliament the best possible image in the defence of the public interest. it underlines our commitment to protecting the environment and to applying equivalent procedures in each member state. it substantially reinforces the commission's well-intentioned but frankly inconsistent recommendations on inspection procedures - recommendations which could not guarantee effective improvements - and provides for a detailed action programme to ensure that existing laws are properly implemented within a realistic but tight timetable. as it stands, this report contains one or two sections which i think could benefit from minor amendments to strengthen them. i have tabled a few amendments and one of the pleasures of speaking for the first time in this house is that one has the feeling that the remarks one makes could be judged on their merits rather than on the political affiliation of the speaker. as mrs jackson has pointed out, the substance of this report and my concern is that the commission might not support these proposals. i congratulate mrs jackson on the work she has undertaken. i am convinced that this report should have the enthusiastic support of parliament and that we should convey to the commission and the council our determination that these essential measures should not be watered down or weakened in any way.
commission - (es) mr president, in fact, in the report presented by mrs jackson there is a point which does not speak so much of the content as of the legal form which can be chosen to try to solve the problem of minimum environmental standards in the member states. the commission has proposed a recommendation. parliament would prefer a directive, not so much, i insist, on a matter of substance, because there is no kind of fundamental amendment to the recommendation proposed by the commission. why did the commission consider that in this case it was preferable to present a recommendation rather than a directive? firstly, mr president, because the commission, before making a legislative proposal, logically consults the member states accordingly. of the 15 member states, only one is in favour of a directive. once again we are faced with a real problem: when the commission proposes a recommendation, you want a directive and when the commission proposes a directive, you have to make recommendations because you have to respect the principle of subsidiarity. it is therefore very difficult, given that 14 of the 15 member states prefer a recommendation, firstly, because sometimes the principle of subsidiarity must be respected; secondly, because we prefer the concept of shared responsibility and thirdly, because this is a measure in a programme which does not exclude, if the recommendation proves insufficient, consideration of the submission of a directive in the future. in other words, firstly, it is simply a pragmatic approach, given that the majority of member states do not want a directive; secondly, the principle of subsidiarity would be invoked and thirdly, the commission prefers to maintain this programme through recommendations, see what the result of this phase of closer cooperation on inspection will be and try in the future, if it is deemed appropriate, to present a directive. these are the explanations i can give you on behalf of the european commission.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i want to come back to this briefly. i take note of the commissioner's argument on subsidiarity, but what parliament wants is a minimum framework directive which does not infringe subsidiarity and solves the problem by requiring member states to set up inspection within fairly broad guidelines. secondly, i would ask the commissioner, since we are all going to put pressure on the member states to change their minds, if he can put us in confidence, in the interests of transparency. which member state should we not put pressure on?

commission. - mr president, it is high time for us all to complete this transitional period: once parliament has approved the new commission, the powers can be transferred to the new commissioners. firstly, i would like to state briefly that the budget is a legal obligation of the commission, in accordance with the treaty. the commission in office must prepare the budget - it has no choice but to do so. i have only a few comments to make on the draft budget adopted by the council: it proposes a reduction of eur 430 million in commitments and eur 1.7 billion in payments. while these reductions are normal at this stage of the budgetary procedure, they are accompanied this year by a substantial redeployment of eur 430 million in category 4 - external actions - to finance the reconstruction of kosovo, which will amount to eur 500 million. if redeployment is necessary to finance this new priority, account should be taken of the fact that excessive redeployment risks destabilising the budgetary and political balance of external relations. the main source of funding for the action in kosovo should therefore be redeployment, but it may be complemented by other means. as regards agricultural expenditure, the new commission will communicate the new forecasts at the end of october in its now traditional letter of amendment, which has been accepted by the institutions. i note the council's overall concern to improve the situation of outstanding commitments, by responding to most of the commission's requests. in category 2 - structural measures - payments can be reduced, in line with the proposal to adjust the advance from 4 to 3.5%: this can be done without too much difficulty. finally, however, i would like to draw your attention to a major illogic in the council's decision. the council proposes to increase the commission's administrative expenditure by only 0.9% while it forecasts a 3.5% increase for the other institutions. the council decided on this reduction on the assumption that the commission would increase the number of vacant posts and thus achieve significant savings. this objective runs counter to the wishes expressed by the european parliament for years and the commitments made by the commission to reduce the number of vacant posts. the key to the success of this year's budgetary procedure is the €430 million for the reconstruction of kosovo and turkey following the earthquake. i am sure that the new commission will make this a top priority and then come forward with a balanced proposal.

- madam president, the presidency of the council has reviewed the main points and identified three areas which the president-in-office spoke about this morning: asylum and immigration, the fight against crossborder crime and the establishment of a european area of justice. i should like to touch briefly on each of these three points. the political challenge in asylum and immigration is balancing the need to protect asylum as an individual right and the need to properly guarantee refugee protection, with the desire to oppose economic migration. europe needs a common migration policy. we need at least some common minimum standards. these standards should be based on the 1951 geneva convention and the unhcr guidelines. we must avoid the lowest common denominator approach, which would weaken the level of protection. the european union must show that it will not become a fortress, fearing infection from outside, but that it will remain a refuge for the dispossessed. the events of recent years have shown us how easily situations of mass refugee flows can arise. tampere must send a clear message that we must separate the issue of asylum from the debate on migration. the temporary protection regime is commendable but only in exceptional circumstances and it should not deny the right to individual examination of asylum applications. let us make sure that we are not re-thinking asylum as a political decision but that we continue to consider asylum as a human right. commission. - mr president, with your permission, i would like to make a statement from the commission on the effects of the financial crisis in russia and on certain aspects of corruption and money laundering. the house should know that the general financial situation in russia has stabilised somewhat since the dramatic fall in the ruble on the international currency markets in august last year. in fact, since the beginning of this year we have seen some encouraging signs, with the recovery of industrial production, mainly due to import substitution, a fairly tight control of inflation and a recovery in the balance of payments, which is mainly explained by a sharp increase in the export prices of russian oil. in addition, at the end of july, russia reached an agreement with the imf and other financial institutions on the resumption of direct borrowing assistance and shortly thereafter another agreement was reached within the paris club to reorganise debt service payments related to russia's public debt. further talks are under way within the london club between private sector creditors. the russian economy has thus had time to catch its breath in the run-up to the duma elections in december and the presidential elections next summer. however, none of these factors alone is sufficient to revive an economy that remains very fragile, with unemployment and poverty levels rising steadily. the authorities responsible must therefore redouble their efforts to encourage a sustainable recovery in the medium term. the adoption by the duma of the government's draft budget for the 2000 financial year will be an important test. in addition to serious structural problems, such as the lack of investment, public debt, especially external debt, is increasing rapidly and it is not clear at present how the authorities intend to deal with it in order to serve the interests of this debt. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud, and i am sure that the commission will take them into account. the commission is aware of the speculation in the media and of the growing concern about the misappropriation of funds from international aid to russia. of course we have to wait for the results of the investigations under way in europe and the united states and of course the commission is following the case closely. in the meantime, the imf, the world bank and the g7 countries being obviously the main donors of direct financial aid, it is primarily up to them to decide how to react to speculation and allegations of misappropriation of funds intended for aid to russia. of course, everyone should be aware that the russian authorities are responsible for the repayment of the aid, including principal and interest. in addition, the latest imf assistance will be absorbed entirely by debt service on the sums russia owes the imf. the operation will therefore consist mainly of a scripting game, without any real transfer of funds. the community's aid, as you know, is mainly provided through the tacis programme, which is managed centrally in brussels. the funds concerned are mainly used to finance european companies to provide russia with their technical know-how and advice. only a very small proportion of the funds is therefore directed to russia. in fact, it is only 4 million euros out of a total of 140 million euros. of course, this 4 million euros is directly managed by our representation in moscow. in addition, the community food aid programme for russia, launched earlier this year, is subject to very close monitoring which includes, among other things, checks on the use of funds generated by the sale of the foodstuffs concerned on local markets. in addition, russia is not currently receiving any loans from the community and the mandate of the european investment bank for loans to third countries does not extend to russia. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the aid is not diverted to the most vulnerable groups. there is also, in the commission's view, the problem of the massive outflow of capital from russia, which is certainly contributing to the low level of domestic investment and thus hindering growth. the commission has always made it clear to russia that a rapid and sustainable reversal of the capital flight trend requires a more favourable investment environment and better protection of investors' rights in russia. the commission has for some time now recognised the link between capital flight and corruption and crime in russia; we also recognize the cumulative threat that these various factors pose to the country's transition to a democratic system and a market economy governed by the rule of law. the house must know that institutional weaknesses and the fragility of efforts to consolidate the rule of law are very profitable for criminal activities. the commission has therefore been and will continue to be useful in supporting russia's difficult transition process through actions focused, in particular, on technical assistance in the fight against money laundering and organised crime, or the promotion of the rule of law in general. i will give the example of this study on russia's institutional and regulatory needs to combat money laundering, which is due to start later this year. in addition, cooperation between russian and commission officials in the field of customs and the fight against fraud is increasing. the house is only too well aware of the extreme skill of the major criminals in exploiting the differences between legal and regulatory provisions around the world and in infiltrating economic and financial systems, without regard to national borders. we are therefore faced with a global problem, which goes far beyond russia's borders. there is no doubt that closely coordinated international action is needed to combat it and the commission is prepared to play its full part in this. the fact remains that russia must do everything in its power to put its affairs in order. the commission therefore hopes that the russian authorities will respond convincingly to what is happening today; it is vital that they cooperate fully with the investigations under way in europe and the united states. the commission notes with satisfaction that the russian authorities have decided to send a high-level mission to the united states to assist the investigators on the ground; i think it's in the works. investigations into these allegations of fraud on russian territory should also be actively encouraged. the commission is, however, concerned that in russia itself the accusations have been denied only in the usual way, without being examined as they should be. in such a context, a timely gesture by president yeltsin to sign the money laundering bill would reassure the international community. the ratification and application of the council of europe convention on this subject is also essential. the commission also hopes that the problems of the russian banking system, which is clearly at the heart of the concerns about corruption, will be resolved quickly. confidence in the banking system must be restored quickly and permanently. this would be a major contribution to a return to a certain degree of normality.
- mr president, allow me to join mr swoboda in his remarks. i did not intend to intervene in this debate, but i listened to the commission's carefully prepared statement, for which i thank mr kinnock. it sums up a situation which i believe is very dangerous and which is developing in russia. what we need now is stability and new investment so that russia can grow, and the exact opposite is happening. in november last year i was in moscow with a group of representatives of this parliament who were sent to assess the humanitarian needs and it became clear that the country is simply not in a position to get its affairs in order. as the european union, we must take a political initiative to try to help the russians get their economy back on track. the countries of central and eastern europe that were part of the former soviet bloc have managed to recover. they have improved their economy and the living standards of their people, and that's because we have put property and property laws at the top of the agenda. this is not the case in russia and the difficulty in that country is, i think, that nobody has ownership responsibility for anything and therefore no real control over the economy. i hope therefore that we will be able to take some form of political initiative to try to get the country to revise its basic legislation.
- mr president, many of us are not too surprised by the reports of the time that the russian central bank has committed embezzlement. we have long known that the considerable sums paid to russia to support the level of the russian economy have not delivered the desired results and that while the top-down approach may have appeared to be the simplest, it may lose its effectiveness over time. we know that the gap between rich and poor has become a chasm, that the russian people have less and less faith in the ideal of democracy, that the infrastructure keeps deteriorating and that workers are not being paid. perhaps the west would have been better off paying teachers, doctors and miners directly. if we are to continue to invest in the russian economy, we must find ways of supporting and developing local economic activities - as our colleague has just said - which can meet the needs of the citizens and give a sense of stability and a form of participation. there are many examples of such actions in the areas of social exclusion, in the poorest countries, from which we can draw inspiration. money laundering and crime are only one aspect of the problem. we need to look at how to develop domestic investment. the example of the west is that you bring in foreigners who make the investments and reap the rewards. we may therefore do well in this house to reconsider certain issues, such as the question of returning profits to the countries where they are produced, instead of simply stripping them of money and natural resources.
- mr president, i would like to begin by congratulating mr kinnock on his second term, which i am sure will be even more successful than the first. the problem we are facing is that while we should not underestimate the damage that crime and organised crime can do to western society, it is important, as far as russia is concerned, to try to look beyond the headlines. after all, to be frank, crime is a fairly common thing throughout russia's history. there's nothing new about it. we must not forget that russia is potentially an extremely rich country. it has huge natural resources, whether it be gold, oil or agricultural land, and yet production has fallen by 50% since 1989. the main problem is that of capital flight, legal or otherwise. all things considered, the money that remains in russia, even if it is on the black market, has an influence on the economy. capital flight now amounts to some us$25 billion a year, while foreign investment is less than us$3 billion and still declining. to be honest, if the russians themselves are not willing to invest in russia, what chance is there for someone else to do it? we must not lose sight of the fact that any contribution from our public money is a mere drop in the ocean. the key to russia's salvation is private investment. that is where we must concentrate our efforts. the answer lies in russia itself. the country must implement the necessary economic reforms. we must have a fair and sustainable taxation system. we must ensure that modern democratic legislation and respect for the law are in place. the industrialists have made it clear to us - for example, at the eu-russia industrialists' round table - that they want to invest in russia. after all, given the potential, there are some great deals to be made in russia by making the right investment at the right time. but they all tell us the same thing over and over again: it's corruption that's holding them back. the investment environment is deplorable, as there is no long-term viable tax system, constantly changing laws, insufficient infrastructure and, above all, unconvincing and confusing property rights, including intellectual property. these are the points on which we must concentrate our efforts. i recognize that in the current climate it is difficult to justify eu technical assistance, but we must continue given the importance russia has for us, both for security reasons and for economic reasons. i was glad to hear from commissioner kinnock. it is important to focus on a few aspects, that is to say, we must not only be interested in improving the economy, but also, of course, in improving civil society, to support economic reform, and in the social aspects. i would therefore ask the new commission - and i am taking advantage of the presence of commissioner kinnock to do so now - to make an overall assessment of the effectiveness of the tacis programme and then to report back to us on what it intends to do to improve the programme in the 2000 budget, so that we can have full confidence when we are called upon to vote in favour of the tacis programme.
- mr president, the earthquake which struck turkey in the early hours of 17 august is the most serious recorded in over fifty years in a region prone to such shocks. the disaster claimed at least 40 000 lives and at this tragic time we express our deepest sympathy and support to turkey. the european union has responded by providing some €45 million in emergency humanitarian aid, which has been been manoeuvring from one end to the other in a twisted, destructive and, above all, shamefully protectionist spirit, seeking from the outset to hold south africa hostage for the benefit of its own subsidised farmers. let me now summarise the main points: the asymmetrical nature of the trade agreement is crucial and implies the systematic reduction of customs barriers and other duties. europe will open its markets to 95% of south african exports within ten years. south africa will open its markets to 86% of european exports in 12 years. this agreement is unique in that it includes the agricultural sector which, of course, is of enormous importance to the south african economy. it also recognises the potential damage that subsidised agricultural products can inflict on south african markets and in fact allows south africa to impose a special safeguard clause if it appears that its agricultural industry is threatened. however, i see the protectionism that unfortunately characterizes the union's common agricultural policy reflected in the agreement. i also believe that this agreement should not be seen as a model, particularly for the acp countries currently participating in the new post-lome agreements. i would like the commission to confirm that this is not its position. but there are clear lessons to be learned about the extreme complexity of such a project, especially when the powerful eu is your partner in extremely bitter and controversial discussions. this agreement must now be translated into practical benefits. in conclusion, let me address the regional implications of this agreement. i think these are the things we fear most. there will naturally be a reduction in customs revenue on which botswana, lesotho, namibia and swaziland have become dependent. these rights can be as high as 90% in the case of lesotho. this will, of course, affect the country's ability to spend on essential health and education and other social sectors. - mr president, the first thing i would like to say is how much i welcome the hopefully successful conclusion of this landmark agreement and i congratulate the rapporteur for working hard to get the best possible result. this free trade agreement is one of the first to be concluded with a developing country and therefore sets a number of important precedents. for example, the agreement does not just focus on trade aspects but extends the field to development cooperation, which i welcome. however, it could set other precedents with less positive repercussions, especially with regard to the impact on other countries in the region. one of the main fears of the countries belonging to the sacu (southern african customs union) is the loss of customs duties, as mrs kinnock mentioned. at present, these countries are heavily dependent on customs duties levied on imports from europe and distributed among the countries of the customs union. this is a very large sum of money. i take swaziland, for example, where 40% of government revenue is dependent on customs duties. however, because of the existence of the free trade agreement, goods from the eu entering the south african market duty-free will also enter duty-free into the other countries of the customs union - there is no customs barrier between these countries. so the sacu countries are really concerned that these products will be sold cheaper than local products within their own markets. while this makes products cheaper for south africans, the effects on local industries can be extremely painful. therefore, there is a strong concern that the pace and scale of removal of customs duties on imports from the eu will exceed the capacity of the region's industries to improve their efficiency. this underlines the importance of properly establishing the successive phases of free trade agreements, in order to avoid negative repercussions on other countries in the region. although compensation for adjustment costs in south africa has been promised for neighbouring countries, how this compensation will be applied is far from clear. the european parliament, i am sure, will continue to monitor the situation, assess the impacts felt by other countries and do everything in its power to ensure that appropriate and necessary compensation is available. the agreement also has wider implications for the post-lome negotiations, in which the commission and the council strongly support regional free trade agreements to replace the lomé-type preferential arrangements. i welcome the recommendations made by mrs kinnock not to regard this agreement as a model for the acp countries. in conclusion, while i welcome the fact that south africa has acquired a significant share of european markets, i hope that we can learn from this agreement and ensure that in the future the phasing out and objectives of these free trade agreements more accurately reflect the diverse needs of the participating countries.

i make a few technical remarks - it seems that she takes her wishes for granted. let me give you a few examples. contrary to what is stated in the report on page 8, the regional safeguard clause does not apply to the whole of the sadc region but only to the blns country which is part of the southern african customs union. since these countries will in practice apply the same customs duties as south africa, it is appropriate to propose the same type of safeguard clause to them but this mechanism does not extend to the sadc region as a whole. the eu has not yet agreed to eliminate customs duties on automotive products from south africa over a three-year period, as the report on page 9 seems to suggest. this option was linked to south africa's efforts in this area, which will be assessed in the second half of 2000. if the south african side proposes a significant opening of markets to the eu, we will be able to eliminate our customs duties completely by the year 2003. otherwise, the eu's liberalisation of the automotive sector will be a long way off. contrary to what is suggested in the report on page 10, the proper management of public affairs is not, in strict legal terms, an essential element of the agreement. this was not part of our mandate as negotiators. however, the agreement states that both parties reaffirm their commitment to the principles of good governance and makes this concept an essential element. however, apart from a few such inaccuracies, the report, as i have already said, is very precise and very well written. i obviously share his positive conclusions. this brings me back to the challenge we still have to face - how we will implement this agreement as quickly and as well as possible. given its mixed nature, we are waiting for the ratification of the agreement by the 15 national parliaments. i hope that the excellent precedent set this week will inspire your colleagues at national level and encourage them to put the agreement on the agenda quickly. however, experience with other agreements has shown that it may be two or three years before the last eu member state ratifies the agreement. in this context, i welcome the fact that the council has decided to apply certain parts of the agreement provisionally, in particular the sections relating to trade and development, as from 1 january 2000. in the coming weeks and months, i will closely monitor the preparation process leading up to that date to ensure that the very important trade concessions granted by the eu to south africa are actually implemented counsel. - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to speak to you today about the current state of the middle east peace process and the role of the european union in this process. it was a pleasure to hear, after several years of silence, positive news on the progress of the peace process. compared to last spring, a lot has changed. six months ago we were in a situation where the implementation of the wye river agreements signed in october 1998 had failed. due to internal political pressure, the israeli government was unable to implement the agreements and the country held early parliamentary elections. the expiry on 4 may of this year of the transitional phase provided for in the oslo agreements has made the situation even more uncertain. the palestinians had announced that they would unilaterally proclaim the birth of an independent palestinian state on that day. at the same time, israel was in the midst of a heated election campaign, and the elements were gathering to make the situation worse. the general atmosphere was one of disappointment and uncertainty. there was also concern that terrorist attacks would increase. today the situation is very different. the outcome of the parliamentary elections and the election of the prime minister in israel in may was the turning point that allowed the resumption of negotiations to resolve the conflict. the new israeli government has convinced the international community that it is serious about peace with its neighbours. certainly, there is still a degree of uncertainty about political developments in the middle east. the difference with the end of last year or last spring is that there are reasons for optimism now. we have evidence of stronger political will, of the ability to conduct direct negotiations and of the timely implementation of signed agreements. i know that the european parliament is closely following the development of the middle east peace process and that there is a lot of competence in this house on issues concerning the region, as demonstrated by the study published in may by parliament on the middle east peace process. i'll focus on the evolution since last spring. it was then, as you know, that parliament delivered its last resolution on the matter. as the country holding the presidency of the european union, finland has logically considered the middle east peace process as one of the most important issues of the common foreign and security policy. we are closely following the peace process and are in close contact with the parties. the finnish minister for foreign affairs visited the region from 1 to 5 august. the president of the republic of finland, mr martti ahtisaari, is currently on a visit to the region, covering israel, the palestinian territories, syria and lebanon. in addition, we found the extensive network of contacts established by special envoy mr moratinos and his expertise in the matter to be of great value. its work has been extremely valuable in terms of obtaining information for the european union, the visibility of the union and contacts for negotiation. the european union has made a significant contribution to the developments of the past few months. we have always encouraged the parties to discuss and negotiate. we have also tried to create the conditions for a climate of opinion favourable to the peace process and we have worked towards détente. a good example of this is the declaration of the berlin european council, which in my view played a significant role in reducing the tension of the spring. the european union has been called on many occasions to be more active in the middle east peace process. and it is true that we are in an excellent position to exert our influence. europe has a millennia-old link with the middle east across the mediterranean and a unique expertise in the affairs of the region. we are not seeking to compete with the us or other players in terms of leverage, but rather to engage in a close dialogue with them. the short-term prospects for the palestinian issue seem to be that the parties will discuss directly with each other, without the significant involvement of other actors. there is a broad consensus among the member states of the european union on the fundamental issues and objectives of the middle east peace process. this consensus has been consolidated over the past decade, making it possible to strengthen the union's role in the region. we are already the largest supplier of aid to the palestinians, which translates into a significant contribution at political level, for example in the meeting of the ad hoc liaison committee which coordinates aid to the palestinians, which will be held in tokyo in mid-october. economic cooperation and the contribution of technical experts in certain permanent negotiation issues and in the field of good administration are areas in which we have been able to provide assistance and are also prepared to act in the future. in addition, the european union attaches great importance to cooperation projects between citizens which bring people together in a concrete way. this cooperation continued in secret even during the years when the peace process was suspended. the current political phase of the peace process can be considered to have resumed thanks to the agreements signed last month in sharm el sheikh. the international community supports the agreement signed by the parties. the implementation of the sharm el-sheikh agreement has been well under way, with israel and the palestinians both scrupulously fulfilling their obligations. the implementation of the agreements through tangible measures is the best way to rebuild the deteriorated trust between the parties. the agreement restores confidence that the principles of oslo have not been forgotten. i think faith and trust will be necessary. the parties have deliberately delayed the resolution of the most difficult and sensitive issues. the one-year deadline set by the parties for the conclusion of a permanent agreement is ambitious. but by taking determined action, by building mutual trust in a systematic way and by adopting a proper attitude, this can be achieved. the european union stands ready to provide assistance with the means at its disposal if the parties so desire. as far as syria is concerned, there is still a real possibility for negotiations and thereby for peace, because both sides want it. it just seems like one of us is waiting for the other to make the first move. we must seize the opportunity, and that is why we are prepared to offer our best services to the parties. i am convinced that the start of negotiations is only a matter of time. the lebanese question seems to have been somewhat sidelined in the rapidly evolving public interest over the past few weeks. from the point of view of lebanon's favourable development, it would be essential to establish more stable conditions in the country. we want the political solution to the lebanese question to move forward at a rapid pace and we are ready to provide our assistance in this area as well, as far as our needs are concerned. i have so far considered the work of peace mainly from a political point of view. the european union plays the most important role in the search for peace, but at the same time, in order to increase confidence and above all to consolidate the peace achieved, economic cooperation and regional cooperation are also important and they will have to be carried out at several levels. this cooperation has not yet succeeded in meeting the expectations set for it as an activity supporting the peace process, but i am convinced that it has every chance of succeeding. this is evidenced by the european union's cooperation with the mediterranean countries in the barcelona process and the activity for the continuation of the mena series of meetings next spring. a just, comprehensive and lasting peace will bring not only changes in regional cooperation but also pressures for internal change within countries themselves. we would like to see the parties prepare the people of their countries for the compromises which the concorde will inevitably force both sides to make. now is no time for harsh words. we firmly believe that change can only be beneficial in the middle east if the fruits of change are harvested. finland, as the current president of the european union, fully understands the possibility of a profound change and will continue, in collaboration with our partners, to pursue peace and the common interest by all available means.
