counsel. - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for this opportunity to present to parliament the council's activities and my views on climate policy. climate policy is one of the biggest challenges facing the environment globally and i believe it will remain so for the next century. climate change will have immense social and economic impacts. of course, they'll be bigger the longer we let the climate change. one thing that people are only now discovering is the likely health effects of climate change. many researchers believe that the increasing number of storms and floods are a symptom of a changing climate. of course, these storms and floods have a direct impact on people's health. but even more significant are the indirect effects of climate change that are due to changes in ecosystems. in many regions, for example, hotter, drier summers are expected to reduce cereal crops. it is also expected that as a result of global warming, many vector-borne diseases, such as those transmitted by insects and rats, will spread. for example, malaria is expected to spread to southern parts of europe and the united states. in total, this can also result in health effects, a new gap between rich and poor, a health gap. this is just one example of the dramatic effects that climate change can bring. that is why tackling climate change, or at least slowing it down, is one of our priorities. the kyoto protocol is a significant step, but it is far from sufficient. it is important to understand that the kyoto commitments must be followed by new commitments if climate change is to be sufficiently slowed down. however, the implementation of the kyoto commitments will be a major undertaking in itself and a major change from what has been done so far. the european union's action has two main aspects. one is the union's own actions to reduce emissions; the other is the union's activity in international negotiations. eu action to reduce emissions is essential, as are national measures taken by member states, if only to ensure the international credibility of the european union. a report by the european environment agency indicates with concern that business as usual will lead to an increase in future emissions in the european union rather than the eight per cent reduction by 2010 we had committed to. this means that new policy measures are needed. one of the most important objectives of the finnish presidency is the implementation of the first sectoral strategies in the fields of energy, transport and agriculture. without such sectoral strategies, it is not possible to achieve the emission reductions we have committed to. in my view, it is important that these sectoral strategies become a continuous process, that is to say that we should not be satisfied with the first versions, but that, on the contrary, these sectoral strategies should be reviewed at regular intervals, for example in the field of transport and energy, and that ever more ambitious objectives should be set. in the international negotiations, i think the most important thing would be to find answers to the questions that are still outstanding, so that we can consider ratifying the kyoto protocol, so that it can come into force and become binding. finland's objective at the fifth meeting of the parties in bonn is to make decisive progress in the creation of rules for the kyoto mechanisms and also in the establishment of rules for the monitoring of agreements. our aim is that, if possible, the fifth meeting should lead to a draft treaty, in which there will of course be unresolved points, but which will enable us to meet the timetable for the treaty to become a reality at the sixth meeting. it is therefore essential that progress be made at this autumn's meeting. one of the most difficult issues is the division of roles between developing and industrialised countries. the finnish presidency will work to ensure that climate policy and development policy can support each other. we are also preparing resolutions in the development council on the respective relations between climate policy and development policy. what is also important for developing countries is, for example, technology transfer. the most important mechanism of these technology transfers will be the cdm, the clean development mechanism. in order for these technology transfers and also the transfers of funds to developing countries to start working, we need rules for this cdm, but it is also important for the european union to make balanced progress in defining all three of the flexibility instruments provided for by the kyoto protocol: the clean development mechanism, international emissions trading and joint application. the 50% ceiling proposed by the european union for the use of flexibility instruments has been the subject of severe criticism from the other contracting parties, which means that it will be a very difficult issue in international negotiations. in conclusion, i would say that the commission's communication on its preparation for the implementation of the kyoto protocol is a clear document and a good start, but it contains mainly preliminary measures. it is also essential to develop a longer-term action programme.
commission - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when the united nations convention on climate change was adopted in rio in 1992, the european union clearly took the lead in relation to the rest of the world. the same was true when the kyoto protocol was signed in 1997. my ambition is to ensure that the eu maintains this role in the fight against climate change. the european parliament has already had the important task of advancing this work. the resolution which has been tabled today is also welcome. this is a huge political challenge. the ratification of the kyoto protocol is not yet within reach. many rich countries, where greenhouse gas emissions exceed acceptable limits, are skeptical. moreover, the largest increases in emissions over the next two decades will occur in developing countries. in the eu itself, the amount of waste is moving in the wrong direction. it has increased considerably in recent years, particularly in the field of transport. it is important to note that by the year 2000 the eu will probably have stabilised its greenhouse gas emissions at 1990 levels, but this is not enough. if we continue at the present rate, we will not be able to meet the ambitions of the kyoto decision to reduce emissions by 8% between 2008 and 2012. this is a bad development, both in the long term and for the eu's credibility on the international stage. how do we meet this challenge? mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as i said at the hearing before this parliament, the fight against climate change is one of my top priorities. i will propose the measures necessary to achieve results in this area. let me start today by mentioning three elements which i believe should be part of an effective and comprehensive climate strategy. firstly, in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, we need a strategy of concrete measures in various areas. a wide range of actors and economic sectors should be involved in this work. to achieve this, i will launch early next year a climate change action programme, the guiding idea of which will be to bring together all interested partners, whether technical experts, business representatives, non-governmental organisations or other key actors. the aim is, of course, to achieve a synergy effect and to try to reach an agreement on the practical measures which the commission may propose to the council and parliament. such a programme could serve as a basis for further measures. an important part of this will be to spread knowledge and make better use of the enormous benefits offered by new technologies. these represent considerable potential, together with renewable energy, new vehicle technologies, and low-energy appliances and machines that are waiting to be brought to market. this potential has not yet been sufficiently exploited. we must draw the attention of a number of people and economic actors to the fact that this new technology also has financial advantages in many cases. the market for these new technical solutions must be expanded, with clear regulation and incentives. secondly, i intend to present a green paper on emissions trading in the eu in the year 2000. i am aware that there are still some doubts about the application of such mechanisms to the flexibility of the system. nevertheless, i am convinced that if they are regulated by a set of effective and clear provisions, they will help to enable us to achieve the necessary reduction in atmospheric emissions at a cost-effective level. thirdly, in addition to these measures, we must also achieve changes in areas which affect greenhouse gas emissions but which are outside the scope of environmental policy. i am thinking in particular of sectors such as energy, transport and industry. that is why we must ensure that the integration strategy adopted in cardiff in june 1998 delivers results. the discussions at the helsinki summit in december will in many ways be decisive for how these sectors can contribute to combating climate change. many people say that all this will take a long time. that is absolutely true, but it is precisely an argument for taking action now. we are seeing some positive developments in some areas. i am thinking, for example, of the efforts made by my colleague, commissioner bolkestein, to remove the obstacles which are holding up the negotiations on the proposed tax on energy consumption. however, it is clear that if some member states continue to oppose this proposal, we will have to look for other solutions. i noted that the european parliament was in favour of the application of the flexibility clause provided for in the amsterdam treaty. this clause gives certain member states the right to take the lead in this area. transport and energy issues are also of crucial importance in the fight against climate change. i will have the opportunity to discuss with commissioner loyola de palacio the objective of doubling the use of renewable energy sources and further improving energy efficiency. we will also discuss the reduction of air emissions from the transport sector. the commission will shortly adopt new guidelines on state aid for environmental protection. my colleague, mr mario monti, is currently studying how subsidies and financial incentives can help to improve the environment and protect our climate. i will also consider whether aid to fossil fuels could be converted to the use of renewable energy and energy saving measures. i would also ask the european parliament to consider what it can do itself, within the framework of its tasks, to integrate climate change issues into the various economic sectors. we need your full support to achieve rapid results in this area. i fully share the view of this house that we should allow citizens to play an active role in this work by providing them with clear and easily accessible information. we will only achieve results if each of us takes his or her share of responsibility for this problem. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the measures i have just mentioned will help to give europe the credibility it needs to continue to lead the crusade for ratification of the kyoto protocol. this ratification should take place as soon as possible after the sixth conference of the parties to the united nations convention on climate change. if our efforts are to succeed, we will of course also need the full cooperation of the member states, who will have to implement the measures to which they have committed themselves. minister hassi has already mentioned the international negotiations which will take place in the near future, in the context of the fifth conference of partners. in conclusion, let me stress the crucial role of the eu as a hub between the us and the developing countries in ensuring that both sides are fully involved in this process and that they implement the measures adopted. i am counting on the full support of parliament and close cooperation to achieve results, which is our common responsibility to succeed and also in the interest of future generations.

the commission regrets this tragedy and hopes that the investigations by the italian authorities will be conducted in a transparent and fair manner. the commission shares the concern of meps and calls on the member states to work with the italian authorities to gather all available evidence to identify the causes of the disaster. the commission would point out that the community does not currently have competence in this area. it is up to the member states to take the necessary measures. the commission is aware, however, that the common use of airspace by different users, both civilian and military, can be the cause of safety problems, as it is already partly responsible for delays and congestion of air traffic. that is why the commission has in the past, in its white paper on the liberalisation of european airspace, advocated that the management of european airspace be centralised and managed by a powerful international organisation for all aspects of its use. the commission also felt that it would be better to entrust this task to eurocontrol rather than to a community body, as national governments would be more willing to accept that this organisation should play a major role in the military use of airspace. at the request of the council, the commission is preparing a communication on delays and congestion in air traffic and will certainly review this issue and propose initiatives in the field of airspace management.

- doc. b5-0141/99 by mr maaten and others, on behalf of the eldr group, on recent nuclear accidents and the transport of dangerous substances; - b5-0150/99 by mrs mcnally, on behalf of the pse group, on the accident at the tokaimura nuclear power station in japan; - b5-0161/99 by mr papayannakis and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on the nuclear accident in japan; - b5-0165/99 by mrs ahern and others, on behalf of the green group in the european parliament, on the very serious nuclear accident in japan and the transport of mixed oxide fuel; - b5-0171 by mrs grossetête and others, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on the nuclear accident at tokaimura in japan;
- every accident is a tragedy for people and, of course, we express our sympathy to the workers affected by the tokaimura accident, their families and the 300 000 inhabitants who had to experience terrible fear for several days. accidents happen in all industries, we just saw in the uk a terrible train accident this week. but accidents in nuclear installations, especially critical accidents, are the most feared. while they are rare, for obvious reasons, their potential consequences for a very large number of people are extremely serious. that is why the nuclear industry must be more careful than other industries. this industry will not survive if the public does not believe in a culture of safety that is firmly inculcated and strictly enforced. this culture has clearly been started this week in tokaimura. there will be an investigation. we hope and expect that the conclusions will be available to all so that lessons can be learned where nuclear activities take place. the staff of this industry expects it, and the public certainly expects it. nuclear activity requires contingency plans, on-site inspections by independent inspectors and the factoring in of the possibility of error or negligence. it's expensive, but it has to be done. all facilities in the supply chain must meet the safety requirements. any weakness is dangerous. those whose concerns have been fully justified by this very serious accident in japan are demanding a full-scale investigation and a public explanation.
- two accidents have caught our attention in the last ten days. the first occurred in tokaimura. forty-five people were injured and three are in hospital in critical condition. the second was the london train accident, in which 70 people were killed and 200 injured, when a train carrying hundreds of passengers from the capital to the region of england i represent. while i share the grief of the victims of the train accident and their relatives, i fear that these two accidents are very different. accidents in transport systems threaten the lives of hundreds of people, and nuclear accidents can unfortunately affect hundreds of thousands or even millions of people. mrs mcnally pointed out that in tokaimura, near tokyo, 300,000 people were unable to leave their homes. it turns out the accident wasn't as bad as we thought. as a former japanese official and as a former member of the japanese delegation for 15 years, i wish to publicly express our concern for the victims of this accident in japan. i would like to make three political remarks. first, it is quite obvious that human error or human stupidity will always affect us in all our activities. we cannot trust any individual. at tokaimura, it even appears that staff - with the active collusion of management or due to management's failure to enforce regulations - have violated regulations designed to ensure nuclear safety. rumor has it there was an illegal management manual that told the staff to work this way. a quick action by the japanese police inside the company would allow us to know if this was indeed the case. if that were the case, it would prove that nietzsche was right when he said that madness is rare in individuals but common in parties, groups and organizations. we therefore need individual and independent controls to monitor what is happening in nuclear power stations. someone has to stop these people from making stupid mistakes. secondly, there is a clear lack of contingency plans. thirdly, we must add that we should offer our help to the japanese if they ask for it. finally, two corrections of fact: firstly, our amendment no 6 makes it clear that when we ask that the plant not be reopened until an investigation has been carried out, we are talking about processing plants and not the tokaimura reprocessing plant, a different plant on a different site, run by a different company...
the commission shares the concern of the european parliament and others about the accident at the japanese uranium processing plant. the fact that such an accident could occur in a technologically advanced country like japan is a reminder that nuclear safety obviously requires extreme vigilance at all times and at all levels. the fact that the managers of a facility handling such hazardous materials were able to obstruct or circumvent procedures designed to prevent such accidents is also a matter of serious concern. this raises in particular the question of the whole safety culture of the plant and the level of training of the staff as well as the importance of rapid dissemination of information. the commission has already requested more information from the japanese authorities on the accident and its causes. the authorities have launched an investigation. it will no doubt cover regulatory issues, safety procedures, supervision and staff training. the commission will analyse the report of this inquiry very carefully in order to draw the lessons for europe. in the light of these lessons, it will review its emergency procedures in due course. poor safety management and a lack of training or qualifications of personnel appear to have played a decisive role in the origin of the accident, as in many others. in the european union, the national authorities of the member states must request commitments to inform exposed staff and apprentices of the health hazards associated with their work and to train them in radiation protection. the commission will ask the member states what their latest provisions are on radiation protection and staff training. the commission will also undertake a study of the current levels of nuclear safety training of operators and other workers in the various types of nuclear installations in the european union. research into safety culture in the nuclear sector is already included in the research and training part of the community's fifth framework programme. research into the safety of nuclear reactors is also included in the programme, although the level of funding is lower than before. the commission will respond positively to any request for assistance from the japanese authorities in the management or assessment of the consequences of the accident. the commission services will remain in close contact with the international atomic energy agency to exchange information and analysis and, if necessary, support monitoring activities. the issues raised in the proposal concerning the manufacture, transport and use of mixed oxide - the mox fuel - are unrelated to the accident at the tokaimura plant. issues relating to fuel inspection at the mox fuel reprocessing plant are the responsibility of national authorities and have been reported to the uk nuclear installations inspectorate. there was no way that any part of the equipment could escape security. the transport of mox fuel shall be carried out under the control of the national authorities of the country of origin and destination, taking into account the relevant community legislation and iaea standards. given that the mox fuel for japan is ready for use by nuclear power plants without further processing, it will not pass through the tokaimura facility. as regards the use of mox fuel in nuclear power stations, this decision was taken individually by the power stations with the authorization of the national safety authorities.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i am changing my hat to present my report to parliament. i would like to thank my colleagues in the committee on legal affairs and the internal market very sincerely for entrusting me with this task one week after i took office and i see that a number of colleagues are here to support me. i'm going to try to make this presentation simple. it is a major legislative act relating to the single market and lays down uniform technical specifications for a fundamental component of fuel tanks in motor vehicles. the proposal achieves four important objectives. firstly, it introduces uniform standards for the testing of plastic tanks; this includes all categories of motor vehicles, namely cars and commercial vehicles. some of you may be aware that the automotive industry is increasingly using plastics. these uniform testing standards will enable designers to concentrate on meeting a single standard rather than dispersing their efforts to meet a whole series of different standards. it is often thought that these technical guidelines do not mean much to consumers. however, i must stress, from my experience as an engineer in the automotive industry, that if engineers were allowed to focus on making safer and cleaner vehicles instead of having to comply with a whole series of different regulations, customers and users would be the ultimate beneficiaries. that is the first objective. the second objective is to extend the provisions on technical specifications in the future through a regulatory committee procedure with a view to introducing new standards for gaseous fuel tanks. it is an important and forward-looking proposal because gaseous fuels are increasingly being used - for example, liquefied natural gas and petroleum gas - and because hydrogen may well be used as a fuel in the future. this is a sensible step, but it took 18 months for this relatively straightforward technical measure to reach the stage of second reading. this does not seem to me to be a very wise use of administrative time. that is the second point i wanted to raise. thirdly, this directive allows the extension of the type-approval to cases where motor vehicles are equipped, after their construction, with additional tanks for supplementary fuel or with additional tanks of larger capacity. once again, this is an increasingly important safety measure. these three main objectives were contained in the original commission proposal which was transmitted to parliament at first reading and which subsequently led to the common position. parliament, at first reading, was particularly keen to add an important additional objective, namely to solve the problem of accidental spills of diesel fuel on the road which are increasingly dangerous for road users, especially cyclists and motorcyclists. parliament suggested that this problem should be tackled. this suggestion was rejected by the commission but the council's common position did contain this measure. the spill is the result of the wrong placement of the tank cap and the directive we are presenting to you, together with the amendments tabled by parliament at second reading to strengthen these provisions, tackles this problem by requiring that motor vehicle tanks be fitted with an effective closing mechanism so that the caps are always tightly closed. we have added recitals explicitly making these points the objectives of the legislation and reinforcing these technical requirements to ensure that the provisions prove effective. i am convinced that we will have the full support of the house. i would like to say, in presenting these points, that this is not the only solution to the problem. our committee also wishes to draw your attention to the fact that other committees should address this safety problem through the forthcoming directive on emissions from heavy commercial vehicles and through vehicle testing standards, to ensure that faulty tank caps are detected, during road checks or the annual technical inspection of commercial vehicles. in conclusion, mr president, the last element of this proposal concerns the committee procedure to maintain and improve the technical nature of this directive, as i said earlier. parliament proposed, at second reading, a change in the comitology provisions but, in the light of the amsterdam treaty, i did not recommend supporting these amendments. i suggest that we adopt the proposal from the council and the commission to accept the regulatory committee procedure. this question will be raised when we discuss mr ferri's proposal later. in conclusion, i recommend this proposal to the house. it is a sensible, straightforward proposal, relating to the single market, with a number of important elements, and i hope that it will have your unanimous support.

commission - (fi) mr president, the draft directive under consideration concerns the compulsory installation of a speed indicator on all new two- or three-wheel vehicles. the commission considers that, for safety and environmental reasons, it should no longer be acceptable for two- or three-wheel vehicles not equipped with an approved speed indicator to be placed on the market. users of two- or three-wheel vehicles must always be able to respect the speed limits in force in the member states. they should no longer be able to invoke the lack of regulation to avoid penalties for speeding. the speedometer is already standard equipment in many vehicles on the eu market, but this does not have a major influence on the overall price of the vehicle. in addition, the compulsory installation of a speed indicator on all the vehicles in question creates major advantages for users. the commission would be prepared to accept all the proposed amendments, but the fifth amendment concerning comitology may prove to be very problematic. as the commission will shortly be making a proposal to amend the framework directive, i.e. the directive which created the committee responsible for vehicles, the commission feels that it would be better to examine the comitology on this occasion. or when the new comitology decision, which was accepted in june, comes into force for the new committees, the case can be considered on that occasion. i would find it regrettable if the document was to be examined in conciliation this time only because of a problem with comitology.
the rapporteur, mr president, would like to thank once again all my colleagues on the committee on legal affairs and the internal market for their support in the preparation of this report. this report was considered at first reading by parliament earlier this year - counsel. - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the examination of the 2000 budget has made considerable progress since i presented the council's draft budget here on 14 september. i have heard detailed views and justifications today on the content of the 2000 budget, particularly from the european parliament's point of view. the union's resource needs seem to be very varied and the key issues to be decided are gradually beginning to emerge. the new practice of trilogue has enabled us to examine many of the central problems in a positive spirit. the speeches also made it clear what the central area of the 2000 budget should be. the emphasis is on several current challenges in section 4 'external actions', which require common solutions from the budgetary authorities. my speech on the budget will first be on a general level and i shall come back to the question of kosovo or the question of section 4 at the end. i would like to comment on the compulsory agricultural expenditure, i.e. subcategory b1. the council's view is that the commission's draft overestimates the requirements for the year 2000. that is why the council, in its own review, reduced this item by eur 375 million. the commission's overestimation was regular throughout the 1990s. this is also reflected in this year's figures. the same can be seen with regard to rural development activities in subcategory b1. the differences between the council and parliament on the appropriations for structural items are exacerbated by two issues: firstly, the amount of advance payments for new structural items and, secondly, the timing of the management of old unpaid commitments. i consider both things to be purely technical. the commission has proposed an advance of 3.5% instead of 4%, but this does not require any amendment of the regulation. nor will this affect the new structural fund resources received by the member states in 2000-01. as regards old commitments not paid, it is necessary to take account of the new information published by the commission. it should also be noted that the level of payment of commitments presented by the commission, at 48%, is well above the floor of 45% set by the berlin european council. in the field of internal policies, there are many programmes which are currently being examined under the codecision procedure. it is important that the budgetary authorities respect the expenditure ceilings agreed in the interinstitutional agreement. this requires ever more effective coordination. there are major pressures in the development of the union's administration. the new commission promised to report on the development of the administration in february 2000. we can already say that it is only on the basis of the views presented by the commission that we can assess the overall staffing needs. in the early stages of olaf's activities, it is necessary to give value to qualitative features. in the matter of pension funds, which parliament has stressed, we must await the commission's report covering in particular the reform of the staff regulations and other concrete proposals. the reform proposed by parliament is so extensive as regards bat that it may not yet be ready for implementation in the 2000 budget. the financing of activities in kosovo and of other external actions is a challenge for the union, both from the budgetary and financing point of view. it should be noted that the immediate financing needs of the kosovo region were considered to be largely covered. this was noted at the first donor conference in july. the budgetary authorities should therefore now await the final assessments of needs which, in my view, should not be reliably met until next year. the council, for its part, undertook to meet the financing needs caused by the earthquake in turkey by means of a loan from the european investment bank, macrofinancial assistance and funds from the meda programme. thus, separate funding for turkey may not be necessary. as far as east timor is concerned, aid has already been channelled through the echo programme. the donor conference for east timor will be held in november, so that more precise assessments can only be made later. as i said earlier, kosovo has become the most important item in the budgetary procedure for the year 2000. that is why the council has shown flexibility in its own way of acting, and that is why appropriations have been readjusted in the draft budget for the reconstruction of kosovo. it would seem appropriate to further adjust the humanitarian aid appropriations, particularly because a large proportion of the refugees have already returned to kosovo and humanitarian aid in kosovo appears to be, on the road to reconstruction and to some extent, the first step in providing people with winter shelter. as regards the appropriations allocated to other budget items, which relate to the 'external actions' of section 4 of the financial perspective, a flat-rate reduction makes it possible to prevent hasty decisions to control the maximum rate of this category, because, as i said, the estimates of the real needs for reconstruction have not yet been provided. as regards parliament's concern about the possible consequences of the readjustment of appropriations in category 4, of the aid provided by the union to the least developed countries, it should be borne in mind that, in accordance with the general agreement of lomé, the european development fund finances eu aid to a large number of these countries. the european development fund is not included in the general budget of the european union, but the member states participate directly in its financing and the edf has its own internal financing rules. the reallocation of resources for the reconstruction of kosovo has therefore not had any influence on the european development fund. sub-category b7 of the budget is only partly allocated to the poorest states and thus a flat-rate reduction is detrimental to more than just the poorest states. the budgetary council meeting on 16 july reviewed the re-adjustment of appropriations for kosovo and found that the commission should not burden the least developed states and the poorest groups, and reiterated the commission's commitment to the international development strategy aimed at halving world poverty by 2015. i have noted that the european parliament also intends to propose appropriations above the maximum rate of section 4 of the financial perspective to use the funds to finance activities in east timor and turkey and to adopt a new fisheries agreement with morocco. i would like to make the following comments on this: the council is very concerned about the situation in east timor, but so far no precise estimate has been given of the amount of aid needed. the earthquake in turkey requires our assistance already this year. such assistance was voted in supplementary amending budget no 4/1999. however, it is too early to determine the overall amount of assistance appropriations needed for the year 2000. the appropriations for financing external action in east timor and turkey should also be found within the framework of the maximum rate in section 4 of the financial perspective defined in berlin. the council has also just accepted that the commission should be authorized to negotiate the fisheries agreement with morocco. the final outcome of these negotiations is not yet known. however, i would remind you that in accepting the draft budget the council also readjusted certain appropriations in category 4 to make a provision for the necessary resources required by the new agreement. finally, i would like to briefly examine the growth of the budget and the overall framework for budgetary preparation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the corresponding figure in the council's draft budget is 2.8%. we are responsible to the european taxpayers. it should be clear that budgetary discipline and cost-efficiency requirements must be respected in union expenditure. the union's budget must follow the strict line followed in the budgets of the member states. i stressed at the beginning the need for the budgetary authorities to react quickly in rapidly changing circumstances. i believe that the new interinstitutional agreement contains sufficient means to meet unforeseeable needs. the spirit of the new agreement is clear: no more money can be requested than the overall amount of the initial financial framework for assistance. let this also serve as a basis for the adoption of the 2000 budget. i believe that with the proper cooperation of the institutions we will successfully bring the draft budget for the year 2000 to a successful conclusion. i thank the president and the members of parliament. the rapporteur. - i am honoured to have been chosen as rapporteur for this important report. the european parliament is called upon for the first time to give its opinion on the progress of the european central bank and it is in this context that i have the pleasant duty to congratulate the ecb and its president, mr duisenberg, on the successes achieved so far. the launch of the euro is in itself a truly historic moment in the life of an extraordinary company. it is a considerable technical achievement and the many officials involved deserve our thanks and congratulations. it would certainly still be a little premature to make a judgment on the results of the ecb's mandate, but we can already point out here today many positive signs, one of the most important being that investors are willing to lend their money to the euro zone governments at very low interest rates. this is a real vote of confidence that the ecb will continue to guarantee price stability and will not allow the erosion of the economies of the citizens by inflation. it is in this context of general support for the objectives of the european central bank and of praise for what it has achieved so far that my remarks should be made. the ecb can only continue to receive the same support in all circumstances, good or bad, if it is transparent about how it takes its decisions. it will still be able to achieve its objective of price stability, but without this openness no one will know whether it was achieved by tactics, and can therefore be repeated, or by a happy accident, this time resulting in the need to improve the bank's working methods. the committee was struck by the fact that other central banks had moved more rapidly towards greater transparency in recent years. the federal reserve, the bank of japan, the riksbank of sweden and the bank of england publish all the votes, including the names of the members who voted for or against, in the committee responsible for interest rates. they all publish forecasts, they all give information about the nature of the debates within their board of governors. in view of these various objective measures of transparency, the ecb is lagging behind the usual international practices. the commission therefore proposes, first, that the ecb publish a concise account of the various views expressed for and against the proposed monetary actions. the commission proposes that the ecb publish forecasts of economic developments in the euro area every six months. the remarks made by mr duisenberg before us today are particularly welcome in this respect, as he has promised to do so within the next year. thirdly, it proposes that the ecb publish regularly an overview of developments in each of the euro area countries in order to have a positive influence on the development of prices and wages, which, as mr duisenberg rightly pointed out, differs from one member state to another. finally, the economic and monetary committee may request to hear the president following each important monetary decision. all these measures would go a long way towards promoting a culture of transparency. there was no agreement in the committee on economic and monetary affairs on a request for the publication of the votes, as proposed in the amendment tabled today by the liberal group. the feeling was that a young institution should be given time to develop. most members felt that the publication of votes would increase public pressure on members of the governing council to vote in accordance with national interests. the commission also did not support the liberal group's view that it would be useful to publish the ecb's econometric models for the euro area, partly out of fear of misuse. the commission has also rejected the view expressed by the greens in their amendment today, that the price stability mandate should be amended to take account of the difficulties of manufacturers alone in the event of falling prices. the epp amendment, however, contributes to the understanding of the paragraph and deserves, in our view, support. mr president, let me now say a few words on several other points we have raised. first, i would like to thank mr duisenberg again for assuring this house that the process of cooperation between the ecb and the national central banks is now in full swing, even in the event of a serious crisis requiring support for a euro area financial institution. secondly, i would stress the opinion of the committee on economic and monetary affairs that the ecb should put pressure on member states which are making excessive use of short-term debt, as this poses risks, particularly in the event of a financial crisis. thirdly, we encourage the ecb to play its full role on the international stage as one of the three main pillars of the international monetary system. fourthly, i very much welcome what mr duisenberg has said on this point in the report about the need to reduce the cost of crossborder payments, particularly when it comes to small amounts which are more of a concern to individuals. mr president, if the euro is a great success, as i hope it will be, it will help to revolutionize the european economy. by helping to complete the european single market, it will give european consumers a wider choice of goods and services of higher quality at lower prices and thus encourage a faster rise in living standards. it will create jobs in the expanding industries, which is the only sure guarantee of future prosperity. i am convinced that the ecb will face many challenges in the years ahead, but this does not detract from the pleasure of my observation today: so far the ecb has responded very dynamically to the challenges it has encountered. we can look forward to a future that adds to his recent successes. runaway success. it remains to be seen whether the one-size-fits-all model of interest rates will work in countries like ireland without leading to large tax increases and undermining the popularity that britain and the british conservative party, to which i belong, have never been hostile to the euro as the currency of those member states which actually wish to adopt it. however, since we are all bound by our membership of the single market, a collapse in confidence in the euro would affect us all, whether we are in the economic and monetary union or not. it is therefore vital that the central bank enjoys the confidence of the financial markets. we live in an era of massive capital flows and huge foreign exchange markets. some 300 billion pounds are traded in the city of london every day. a collapse in the credibility of the system, or the sudden conviction that the bank is not in a position to pursue an anti-inflationary policy at any cost, could have serious economic repercussions throughout the union. i believe that only the central bank should, for example, decide on exchange rate guidelines for the euro, if necessary, in order to avoid sending contradictory messages to the financial markets. i also think it is vital to encourage the bank to follow the example of other major central banks, such as the us federal reserve, and to make transparency a key - mr president, everyone, and especially a lawyer like myself, is in favour of justice and civil rights. any eu member state or candidate country should already have systems for protecting its citizens based on its own customary law, case law and legislation. the third pillar is the vital repository of national competences arising from historical development and reflecting the cultural and social specificities of nations. i think that to demolish it at the very moment when it could be of the greatest service would be sad and deeply wrong. as far as the immigration and asylum proposals are concerned, i was the british minister responsible for these matters until 1997. based on this experience, i now believe that at the global level, the uncontrolled movement of people over the next 20 or 30 years, whether it is due to economic or climate issues, represents a colossal challenge to order and democracy. i am certainly in favour of freedom of movement within the eu where there is a legal status but what about the candidate countries and their borders - will they have to take over the protection of the eu, in accordance with the schengen provisions? are we really satisfied with these arrangements and is tampere really addressing these issues? what do our german friends think? what do the voters in yorkshire or brentwood in the uk think? the right to asylum is a precious asset which must not be abused, as is unfortunately very often the case. the 1951 un convention was clear: it must be applied to the letter but must not be replaced or framed by new regulations which, in my view, could only increase confusion. sometimes, if we want to be generous, if we want to be sensible, it's essential that we also be firm. i regret that tampere does not address these issues with sufficient firmness.
- mr president, my group welcomes the publication of the report by mr dehaene, mr simon and mr von weizsäcker, because it clearly and accurately presents the argument for the need for an intergovernmental conference which goes beyond the famous 'three issues left on the table in amsterdam'. we need to address the problem more broadly. the igc will not, however, aim so much at extending the scope of responsibility or the powers of the european union as at initiating structural and institutional reform, which will make the union more open, more efficient, more democratic and more transparent. the igc will be able to function and assume its responsibilities when it is composed of more than 20 member states. the three issues left on the table in amsterdam will be part of the reform package but they will not be the only ones. we are winning the debate on the enlargement of the agenda. however, as mr barnier has pointed out, these three issues alone are not easy to deal with. for example, the extension of qualified majority voting will immediately lead eurosceptics of all stripes and others to say in their respective member states that their country is giving up its right of veto and sovereignty. indeed, one of the largest groups in the epp is of the opinion that qualified majority voting should not be extended. but if they would take a minute to think about it, they would soon realise that their own country, that each country, loses more by the vetoes of other countries than it gains by using its veto in many areas of the european union's responsibility. however, the only three issues which remain on the table in amsterdam, namely the extension of qualified majority voting, the size of the commission and the weighting of votes in the council, do not require changes. changes are needed in the court of justice. how will it function if it is made up of almost thirty members? changes are needed in the size of this parliament if we are to respect the limit of 700 members laid down in the treaties at our express request. something must be done to follow up the conclusions reached by our member states on the necessary integration of the weu and the transfer of its functions, or part of its functions, to the european union. there is also the question of the codification and simplification of the treaties, a question which our parliament was the first to raise on the eve of the amsterdam negotiations. this task has been started in amsterdam but is far from complete. this is also a point raised and emphasized by the dehaene report. the addition of new subjects such as these to the igc does not necessarily complicate it. a broader package of measures could facilitate the conclusion of an agreement and ratification by the member states, but on behalf of my group i can say that we are keen to see parliament working closely with the commission, in the spirit of what mr barnier has just said, so that we can put on the igc table a balanced package of proposals which the commissioner and our representatives can defend at all igc meetings: a package which will enable the union to work when it has more than twenty member states.
- mr president, i welcome this report because it draws our attention to the central question of how the treaties will be revised in the future. we must realise that it will be almost impossible - and certainly unrealistic - to reach agreement between 25 or 30 member states on fundamental sovereignty issues. the main reform therefore concerns article 48 on the amendment of the treaties. we must consolidate the constituent articles of the treaty and have a more flexible, lighter system for amending the treaty in respect of the political chapters. the first reform will be designed to allay citizens' fears about gradual transfers of sovereignty and the second should encourage them to commit themselves more clearly to the political choices we face in brussels and strasbourg. the second essential reform is to remove the right of national veto from the provisions on enhanced cooperation and the third is to grant citizens the right of direct access to the european court of justice.

in writing. - i welcome this first annual report by the governor of the european central bank, mr duisenberg. he deserves our praise for the successful establishment of the ecb and the smooth introduction of the euro. for meps like myself, the ecb's annual and monthly publications have proved to be very valuable and of a very high standard. i regret, however, that the ecb does not follow the high standards of transparency and openness set by the bank of england. the bank of england was granted operational independence in may 1997, one of the first acts of the labour government. the minutes of the meetings of its monetary policy committee are now published within a period of about six weeks, including the minutes and explanations of votes. this strengthens the confidence of the markets in its decisions and is an example of transparent management. it is certainly no coincidence that since the courageous decision taken by the labour government in may 1997, britain has enjoyed an unprecedented period of economic stability and has been praised by the oecd. it is also no coincidence that this decision by the labour government was criticized at the time by the ever-fluctuating conservatives, whose record of economic instability and incompetence is unmatched. i would like to see the ecb apply a policy of openness and transparency similar to that of the bank of england. such a policy would include the publication of the minutes of its governing council with explanations of the decisions taken, particularly on interest rates. it would be upsetting for britain to go from being open to being relatively secretive. therefore, if britain were ever to join the euro, the ecb would have to opt for more openness.

in writing. - mr president, most of the voters in my constituency were probably unaware that an important meeting of eu governments was taking place in tampere last week to discuss justice and home affairs issues. it is perhaps because the agreements reached are so common sense and so clearly beneficial to ordinary british citizens that even the most europhobic conservatives could not object and could not protest. alongside other measures, eu governments also agreed to create a common area of justice to deal with organised crime, in particular drug trafficking and human trafficking. crossborder police cooperation will now be increased, including - following a suggestion from the uk - the creation of a task force of police chiefs and a european police academy. there will also be greater crossborder judicial cooperation including mutual recognition of court decisions across eu countries. accelerated extradition procedures will be introduced, which could even help bring former dictators to justice. in addition, measures were agreed in tampere to make it easier for ordinary citizens to move, live and work throughout europe. third country nationals who have been long-term residents in britain, for example those from the commonwealth, will now be guaranteed equal access to education, health care and other benefits on the continent. in addition, uk nationals facing legal difficulties abroad will now have easier access to justice, including access to legal assistance and translation services and simplified compensation and claims procedures. among other measures, governments also agreed on common rules for the reception of persons requiring political asylum and the drawing up of a charter of fundamental rights. the charter will, for the first time, list all the fundamental rights granted to eu citizens in a single document. this landmark document will complement the european convention on human rights which the uk government has just incorporated into uk law. all these measures will ensure that i am not left in the lurch when constituents in my constituency who are facing legal problems abroad come to me for help. the british will now have the same statutory rights on the continent as all other eu citizens. the british, who were for so long relegated to second-class citizenship under conservative governments, are now first-class citizens under labour.
- mr president, let me first of all support the epp's argument and say that this debate is mainly about a company in a member state and therefore not a matter for the eu institutions to deal with. the challenge to michelin in terms of competition forces it to increase productivity, which means redundancies. i understand we're dealing with a bicycle tire factory. let 's see . michelin can import bicycle tyres at half the price of french production. no business can survive under these circumstances. the question is whether we want europe to be a bicycle-tyre economy or a modern high-tech economy. i would like to question a prevailing idea in this house, and in particular in the committee on employment and social affairs. it is claimed that we could save jobs and improve job prospects by discouraging companies from laying off workers they no longer need. an idea that may seem plausible but is completely wrong and goes against the goal. if we keep jobs on life support that are past their expiry date, we are damaging productivity and reducing the competitiveness of european industry. we keep workers in a deficit and value-destroying situation instead of offering them the freedom to find new employment in a profitable sector where they can create wealth. under the flexible anglo-saxon model, workers frequently lose their jobs, but this is of no consequence because they quickly find another one. (various movements) under the rigid and sclerotic european social model, we fight to keep workers in failing companies and when they finally lose their jobs, they may be unemployable. that is why europe has much higher unemployment, and long-term unemployment, than the united states. finally, we should remember that governments do not create jobs, that the european institutions do not create jobs. businesses create jobs. as legislators, our task is to create an environment that allows businesses and employment to flourish. we should not ask industry to formulate social protection objectives. let governments take care of social security and let industry create wealth and jobs.

commission - at the florence summit in june 1996, the heads of state and government agreed to lift the embargo against the united kingdom 'only and exclusively on the basis of objective public health and scientific criteria and when the commission considers, in accordance with the existing procedures, that these criteria are met'. the implementation of the export regime involves high requirements. first, the uk had to slaughter calves and heifers born of known bse cases - which would otherwise be eligible - before the export scheme could come into force. any new animal showing signs of bse is also slaughtered. secondly, the only products eligible are: boned meat and a limited range of derived products from animals aged between 6 and 30 months and born after the ban on animal flours, i.e. after 1 august 1996. in addition, not only are the animals and their mother subject to strict conditions of identification and traceability, but there must also be sufficient guarantees that the mother has not contracted bse. finally, the entire production chain must be subject to strict specific controls and must be in full compliance. these controls are the responsibility of the uk authorities. however, before fixing the date on which exports under the scheme were to resume, the food and veterinary office carried out a mission to verify the implementation of the export scheme. the mission was successful and the resumption of exports was set for 1 august 1999. the uk has already carried out two audits of dbes controls this year alone. these inspections took place in april and october. the opinion issued by afssa on 30 september 1999 concerning the lifting of the embargo on beef and beef products originating in the united kingdom reaches an unfavourable conclusion. this opinion is based on scientific and control arguments. the scientific questions were submitted to the scientific steering committee for its opinion. preliminary meetings were held on 14 and 25 october 1999 in the framework of the esb ad hoc group. during these meetings, the scientific documentation provided by afssa was reviewed and maff epidemiologists were again consulted. a report from these meetings, which explained the situation in detail, was presented to the scientific steering committee. this committee met in brussels yesterday and is still meeting today to discuss the matter and to issue an interim opinion. the meeting is not over yet. so i have no information yet on the outcome of this meeting. i understand that my colleague, commissioner byrne, will present the conclusions of the meeting of scientists at a press conference with the chairman of the scientific steering committee at 6 p.m. in brussels this evening. i can assure you that the european parliament will be kept fully informed of the findings of the scientific steering committee.
- madam president, the united kingdom has complied with the demands of the florence summit and that is why i say that france must immediately lift the embargo on british beef. the florence agreement concluded by the heads of state and government of the european union on 21 june 1996 sets out five preconditions which the united kingdom must meet in order to lift the embargo on its meat exports: the implementation of a selective slaughter system; the introduction of an effective and fully operational system for the identification and traceability of animals; and legislation on the removal of meat and marrow from feed and farm composition. the united kingdom meets all these conditions, which the rest of europe does not. the fourth and fifth conditions respectively consist in the effective implementation of the 'over 30 months' rule, i.e. the exclusion from the food chain of any animal over 30 months of age and therefore the introduction of improved methods of disposal of specified risk material from bovine carcasses. these conditions have been met by the control measures described above. the european commission inspection visits verify that the uk meets all these conditions. that is why i call for the immediate lifting of the embargo on british beef exports. i think the commission has accepted that british beef can be safely exported. the commission lifted the embargo on british meat on 1 august. the key point is the absence of bovine animals older than 30 months in the uk food chain. there has not been a single case - i mean not a single case - of bse in animals born after 1 august 1996 in the united kingdom, that is very important, no animals older than 30 months in the food chain and no case of bse in animals born after 1 august 1996. there was selective slaughter of cattle born and raised with bse infected animals. the offspring of bse-infected cows must be slaughtered. the cost to british farmers is enormous. in 1995 alone, uk exports to the eu amounted to £500 million, almost half of which went to france. almost half a million calves were exported from britain to the rest of europe in 1995. the message is clear. the cost to farmers of the reduction in the value of british cattle and cattle products and the associated regulations is estimated at £1 billion. while bureaucrats and politicians quarrel, british farmers and their families suffer. on 1 august the commission lifted the embargo; 12 of the 14 member states to which britain could export have lifted their embargo. if france had new evidence concerning the safety of british beef, why did it not inform the commission before the embargo was lifted in august 1999 - why did it wait until today and why is it indefinitely delaying its lifting of the embargo? the british expect france to comply with community legislation and they also expect the european commission to act firmly to end the illegal embargo on british beef. the single market is the very essence of the european union and france's illegal action discredits the whole single market. a war of words over who has the healthiest meat in europe would only undermine consumer confidence in european food, wherever it comes from. we learned this lesson when the first cases of bse appeared. the longer this debate goes on, the more likely it is that british consumers will boycott french food. this is unleashing passions in britain and the crisis must be resolved quickly or we will be going into retaliatory action on both sides of the channel. three months after the commission lifted the embargo, the veterinary committee is still looking for evidence of the safety of uk meat. this is unacceptable. the commission declared uk beef to be healthy on 1 august when it lifted the embargo. it must now take firm action and force france to lift immediately its illegal embargo on british beef. the french government must pay compensation to the british cattle industry for the damage it has caused. the longer this illegal action by france lasts, the more it will damage the reputation of the european union as a whole.

- mr president, it is regrettable that our debate today is again taking place in the absence of a decision by the committee which is currently meeting in brussels. it is also regrettable that this debate has taken such a hysterical turn in some parts of europe, fuelled by some media, particularly those based in london. we all agree that food security and public health must be considered the top political priority in europe. but british beef, as commissioner fischler has repeated today, meets the public health criteria set by the european union. i wonder if the commissioner can state in his summary speech that the raising and slaughtering of cattle is now of the same quality in all the member states. i also regret that this issue has been turned into a battle between france and britain, because this is a matter that france has to deal with europe. the british beef industry has just been through a very tough period where the conditions set by the european union were very severe. those conditions have been met. the commission must therefore take firm action to enforce the lifting of the embargo on british beef. my colleague, mr graefe zu baringdorf, has referred to 'british' beef several times in his speech, but the united kingdom is made up of four distinct regions. and in my home region of scotland, cattle farmers have every reason to feel wronged, because originally they had no serious bse problem. the conditions set by the european union have been met, and yet we are still not able to export our products. our farmers rightly wonder why they have suffered so much to meet these very harsh conditions. what is the point of prolonging this debate for years and setting up a european food agency if its recommendations are not implemented? - mr president, like mr graefe zu baringdorf, who spoke earlier, i was a member of the special committee of inquiry for the esb. he would agree with me that we have added, if i remember correctly, a whole series of special precautions which were deemed necessary to ensure that british beef could once again be considered healthy. these measures, together with the five provisions of the florence agreement, have all been enacted. it was only then, after a three-year period, that the beef embargo was lifted in strict compliance with the conditions described by others in this debate. the logic of the case before the special scientific committee is that we should reject its previous hearings and re-introduce the beef embargo in the european union. what else could the scientific committee say if it were to back down now? one thing is certain, we must strengthen the precautionary principles introduced in the uk following the bse disaster. this implies a review of the current situation and not a retrospective, and it implies looking at how to integrate additional safeguards and precautions after they have been established and further emphasising the urgency of some of them, in particular ante-mortem and post-mortem testing of livestock. some people have already said in this debate that we need to create a european food agency that would look at the kind of health precautions we need. this would imply the introduction of certain conditions which do not yet exist in other european countries. this would involve the removal of meat and bone meal from the entire animal and poultry food chain. this is not the case everywhere. this means strict separation of products at risk. again, this separation is not fully effective. this implies strict precautions against illegal practices of the kind that the commission very quickly discovered with the case of the infiltration of the bovine food chain by human and animal waste, which has just taken place in some other countries. the precautionary principle must be the inspiration for our policy, but it must be based on common principles, a hierarchy of standards which makes health values prevail. the uk government was therefore the first to introduce the concept of a european food agency, while europe is still discussing it. therefore, the dbes specifically excluded anything that was or still was in doubt, including boned meat. mrs roure has pointed out the dangers of xenophobia in this debate. i want to pay tribute to him for his speech. he was a proponent of cordial relations. it would be terrible for us at this stage to sink into chauvinism on either side of the channel. i agree with the president of our national farmers' union who said this week that what upset him most were people trying to make a petty political profit from the tragedy that engulfed his own members. the dispute between two member states over this unilateral embargo could be a disaster. it is likely to be detrimental to the single market. it will cause job losses in the event of sanctions and reciprocal embargoes; and it will humiliate us if we arrive in seattle deeply divided and displaying a belligerent attitude, when we need to stand united against the united states. we understand that commissioner byrne is leaving dublin today and returning to brussels to chair a press conference with mr pascal when the special scientific committee reports. commissioner byrne knows exactly what the ins and outs of this problem are for the commission and european cooperation. commissioner fischler, i would like you to help him understand the sad line from one of his national poems which says that the best lack conviction and the worst are animated by intense passion. we want that intense passion to drive the best in this case. we want people to come together and help europe to act in the way that parliament, the special committee of inquiry, has asked. this is the only way to prevent europe from degenerating and ultimately damaging the european idea in the first place.
- mr president, i certainly enjoyed listening to some of the speeches today, and in particular mr donnelly's opening speech which seemed to criticise the failure of the french and british governments to find a solution to this escalating trade war. i will remind mr donnelly that both these governments are socialist governments. we have just learned that the british agriculture minister has not even met his french counterpart, which is ridiculous when you consider the unleashing of passions in this trade war. but i can understand in part the rage felt by farmers and consumers in britain when they hear that sewage sludge has been incorporated into animal feed in france, when they hear that the british government has been aware of this practice since june but has decided not to raise the issue with the european commission and when they hear that britain still slaughters 60,000 head of cattle over 30 months old a month but cannot pass them through the food chain. otherwise, they are perfectly healthy animals which are incinerated after being slaughtered and their ashes scattered in landfills. this will be considered one of the greatest agricultural mistakes of the century. we are furious to learn that france is also affected by bse - 22 cases have been reported this year. yet even injured and sick animals that die on farms are processed and their wool is introduced into the pharmaceutical industry, the cosmetics industry and therefore into the food chain. as other speakers have said before me, the rules of the game are not the same for everyone. i hope we can find a diplomatic solution, and we must do everything in our power to do so. i call on the commission and the uk government to put pressure on france to comply with the conclusions of the scientific steering committee later this afternoon, whatever they may be tonight.
commission (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to thank you for the way in which this debate has been conducted here today. i think that this was an exemplary debate which can make a considerable contribution to bringing the discussion back to an objective basis. the main conclusions i draw from this are as follows. firstly, i am deeply convinced that in future we must base our decisions, and also those of the commission, on the judgement of independent scientists - and this is very important - and on the latest scientific knowledge. so remember, the origin of the whole bse problem has been precisely the failure to respect this principle, because decisions have been taken for economic and market reasons, without proper consideration of the health issue. that is why we must not make the same mistake again, either way! it would therefore also be wrong to draw conclusions now, without knowing what scientists are currently debating. we must await the opinion of the scientific committee, which is composed of totally independent scientists. but we must also, and i take this very seriously, act immediately. our activities cannot therefore be confined to waiting, and i am happy to convey my message to president prodi and my colleague mr byrne. i am quite prepared to ask them to allow this debate to continue on wednesday, including the commission's conclusions. four key elements were addressed in this french expert report. one is the use of the tests now available. i do not think that these tests should be used purely as a placebo, i think that here too we should base the decisions - which we have done - on a scientific basis. i am convinced that these tests can be of good use in monitoring the whole process at european level, and they should also be used for this purpose. as regards the extent to which they can be used, we must at least be careful about one thing and not think that we have absolute certainty, that we can be one hundred per cent sure that we can distinguish between meat which is dangerous and meat which is not. these tests are good, but they are not 100% reliable. we cannot hope for zero risk here either. if new recommendations are to be made by scientists, we are of course quite prepared to consider them accordingly. as regards control, i agree with those who have said here that the level of control must be comparable at european level and that it is not enough to have an effective control system in britain alone. however, we are not only carrying out inspections in britain but also in other countries, in order to guarantee this principle at european level as well. as regards the request for the establishment of a food agency, i would like to say that we are well advised to move forward on this matter. here the conditions must be defined by my colleague mr byrne, and in this connection i would like to stress again that i am against our going to a food agency such as the fda. i think we should rather take as a model the food agency we already have for pharmaceuticals, a sort of european model of a food agency. as regards the question of postponing labelling, i would like to point out that the commission's interest is not in postponing labelling, but that our interest is not to find ourselves at the end of the year without an optional labelling system and without a mandatory labelling system. there is one point which you must not overlook: it is useless to make a labelling system compulsory in the absence of the necessary database. it is then that we would deceive consumers by presenting them with something that does not exist in reality, and that would undermine our call for transparency and objectivity. in conclusion, in the future, we should really focus on letting the facts speak for themselves. in this way we should also prevent various emotions and, as far as the facts are concerned, we must also be competent and transparent here. in conclusion, i would like to point out that we will be providing all members with the committee's conclusions again today in electronic form.

commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the commission, i should like to begin by sincerely thanking parliament for its overall positive assessment of the new protocol on the fisheries agreement with angola. except for an extension of tuna catches, this protocol takes over the fishing opportunities of the previous protocol for the years 1996 to 1999 and its annexes. it should also be noted - and this was also noted by various speakers - that the protocol has a duration of only one year, and that half of that period has already elapsed. however, the community and angola may redefine the future framework of their fisheries relations during the year, as angola has requested. so we should use that time. the financial compensation paid by the community to angola for the fishing opportunities granted under the protocol and the amount paid by community shipowners in the form of fees also remained unchanged. the financial compensation corresponds, therefore, to the amount fixed in the previous protocol, in proportion to one year. as regards parliament's amendments, i would like to assure the committee on fisheries of parliament on behalf of the commission that we will keep you duly informed of the implementation of the protocol, as we have done in the past. to do this, however, we should choose the most appropriate formulation.
