commission - madam president, i am pleased to have the opportunity today to inform parliament of the developments in the last few days in relation to bse. first of all, i should like to inform you of the opinion adopted unanimously by the scientific steering committee last friday. the opinion concerned the scientific reasons for the advice of the french food safety authority (afssa) concerning the measures applicable to exports of uk beef. i have made sure that the summary recommendations of the scientific steering committee's opinion are sent to parliament on friday with a copy of my press statement. i also made arrangements yesterday for a full copy of the report to be provided to you. however, you may not have had time to digest its contents, so i will briefly summarize the main points. the opinion deals in particular with three questions from the commission. these questions can be summarised as follows: - is there any new evidence in the documents provided by afssa? - should one or more of the four opinions of the scientific steering committee be revised as they directly concern the scientific justification of the date-based export regime? - is the programme satisfactory as regards the safety of the meat and meat products concerned? in its opinion, the scientific steering committee confirmed that the decision to lift the embargo on british beef exports should not be reviewed. let me quote three of the committee's most important conclusions: 'there is clear evidence of continued progress in the decline of bse cases in the uk in 1999. the suggestion that there is a new route of contamination is not justified at this stage.'; - 'the scientific steering committee concludes that there is currently no reason to revise the overall conclusions of the opinions of the scientific steering committee directly concerning the justification of the export regime'; and finally 'the scientific steering committee believes that the measures taken by the united kingdom make any risk to human health from the uk export regime at least comparable to that of any other european member state'. this followed a very thorough examination, which focused on the concerns raised by the french authorities. the unanimous opinion of the committee was very encouraging. it has provided the necessary assurance that the export regime is sufficient to ensure the safety of uk beef exports. and let me be clear: i have always insisted that this opinion of the scientific committee would play a key role in the way the commission would deal with this conflict. on several occasions, including during my hearings before this house, i have publicly stated that my decisions on food safety will be based on scientific evidence. my priority is to ensure there is no threat to public health. sound, independent and excellent scientific advice is essential in this regard. in this particular case, we now have scientific support for existing control systems. it is on this basis that i have asked the french and german authorities to take the committee's opinion into account and to lift their national restrictions on imports of british beef. as i said on friday, these restrictions are no longer necessary in light of the protective measures in place. we must admit, however, that this is a very sensitive subject in which we must proceed with caution. that is why i also stressed on friday that everyone needs a few days to reflect on all the implications of the opinion of the scientific steering committee. the meeting i had last night with my french and british counterparts was in that spirit: we must discuss the best way of resolving this conflict. the french authorities have now requested clarifications on five key points. very briefly, they want more information on traceability, testing, derivatives, controls and labelling. i do not think that this request for clarification is unreasonable. as a result, a meeting of officials will be held this friday to discuss the issues in question. let me quote the very short communiqué on which all the participants agreed last night and which recognises this strategy: 'we have formulated a methodology for getting out of the crisis as quickly as possible by identifying five points - which i have already mentioned - which deserve to be examined by our experts in the coming days. our experts will start this work on friday. we are undertaking this work in a constructive spirit and with a shared commitment to protect the public health of our citizens". i'm very surprised at the press reaction to last night's developments. this is not a setback. this is not a victory for france or a defeat for the united kingdom. it is simply a further step in solving this difficult problem. a few more days of discussion is a very modest price to pay for a happy ending. of course, the alternative - legal action - would be much longer and more painful. further guarantees or clarifications may be necessary to enable the french authorities to lift their restrictions on uk beef. this should not, however, be an insurmountable problem and it is in this spirit that the discussions should continue. the clear implication of these discussions is that the embargo will be lifted. however, i would like to make it clear that there is no question of rewriting the date-based export regime. this programme has been supported by the scientific steering committee as a set of reliable protective measures which ensure the safety of british beef exported under this programme. you can't change it. finally, i will continue to insist on the need for a solution to be found very quickly. i would remind you that this is the first working day since the scientific steering committee's opinion was adopted. we've all worked very hard and worked very hard over the last few days and that effort will continue until we find a solution. i will of course continue to keep parliament fully informed of developments.

commission - (el) mr president, we have just had a very interesting debate and i will begin with a political observation. i think it is just as dangerous to embellish and magnify an initiative by raising hopes as it is to denigrate it by creating a feeling of futility or discouragement. i therefore think that we must give the macroeconomic dialogue its true dimension. it is not an event or a process that we expect to change the reality in the european union. but it is an innovation, an unprecedented attempt to bring together economic actors who have never before been able to sit down together. it brings together those responsible for monetary policy - the european central bank - the political forces of europe, which are represented by the council and the presidency, and the social partners, who represent the forces of production and labour. the participants thus cover a full range. as members of a new parliament and a new commission, we have to implement a decision which was taken before us by the cologne council, and i think we have the political will to develop this dialogue, to organize it, to give it a different form, after having put it to the test, having learned the first lessons and seen in which direction it should be turned. i would like to stress that the macroeconomic dialogue, as outlined in cologne, is essentially about the need to link up growth and employment. and it is one of the key issues in europe today to consider and implement for the first time a european employment policy. the participants in the dialogue, whether at technical or political level, have on their agendas issues of major interest: structural unemployment, longterm unemployment, youth unemployment, initiatives taken in the context of employment policy, the 22 guidelines and action plans of the member states in this field, which are the expected results. the restructuring of the labour market, the restructuring and reforms to be applied, in accordance with the decisions of the cardiff summit, to the product and service markets, can all of them create the conditions for monetary policy to be placed in a different framework? on the other hand, can the single currency, the current low inflation rate and the expected growth rate create a favourable environment for job creation, which is a priority objective of the european union? a dialogue of this kind, which takes place twice a year according to these procedures, cannot provide answers to such crucial questions. but i think we should look at the positive side of this from a political point of view: the issue which concerns the peoples of europe so much - because all the members who represent the peoples of europe have spoken in this debate on their behalf - the burning question of employment and unemployment is at the very heart of the macroeconomic dialogue. in other words, central bankers, finance ministers, industrial associations on the one hand, and labour ministers and the social partners representing the trade unions on the other, discuss and put the question of work at the centre of common policy. i think that for that reason alone we must give this dialogue a grace period, see how it develops and what results it produces before stigmatising it and trying to change it before it has even begun.

the commercial and civil law systems which exist in all our member states were essentially established in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in response to the industrial and commercial changes which had taken place in those countries. we need new responses, responses of our own, for the 21st century. i have expressed, as have other colleagues, our concern about the combined contents of the framework directive on electronic commerce and the revision of the brussels and lugano conventions. some fear that e-commerce may be hampered from its inception by regulations that risk exposing traders to 15 different european jurisdictions and that these same regulations may not actually provide citizens with easy and affordable access to justice. the old conventions and legal approaches need to be given new imaginative thought if we are to really unlock the potential of e-commerce. some have suggested a new lex mercatoria. maybe it should be an e-lex. it is also true, in view of the question by mrs palacio vallelersundi, that parliament must be fully involved in this process. with new legislative proposals, we should not be pushed to deliver opinions and reports at a frenetic pace, leaving us little time to reflect and consult stakeholders and citizens. whether it is such regulation or new flexible legislative methods, parliament must be fully involved in this process and in an appropriate way. there is no room for evasions or lack of clarity. the new trade will need a new framework that offers certainty to both the consumer and the trader. we have challenges ahead. give this house the time and the mechanisms to respond in a way that meets the expectations not only of european citizens but also of the players on the world market who are waiting for us to take the initiative.

- mr president, there are many tragedies that shake our world, but none are as moving as those that affect children. none is as dramatic as the one we heard about today, namely the trafficking of children. i want to refer to one of these trafficking cases, the one involving the adoption sector. in the 1960s, there were 25,000 registered adoptions in the uk, of which 12,500 were of children under one year of age. in the 1970s, these figures had fallen to 13,000 adoptions, of which 3,000 were children under one year of age. in 1990, there was a further drop with 7000 adoptions, including 900 children under one year of age. the differences are largely explained by the widespread and more liberal practice of abortion. in britain, one in five pregnancies is aborted; in london, one in three. with more and more children being put up for adoption with disabilities - physical, mental, or behavioral - it is not surprising that some couples are looking elsewhere for a child to adopt. and in other places, there are babies available for adoption. our first duty is to put the best interests of the child first. when it comes to finding a family for a child, the preference is given to the child's natural family, if the child does not have one, then a family from his own community is chosen. if that's not possible, we'll take a family from a different environment but from the same country as the child. here, if no family is available, then, and only then, will we begin to look for a home abroad. however, it should be a loving and carefully controlled home, and the couple who will be responsible for the child should accept the child's past. the system has too often been abused and the couple's desires often put before the child's interests. so there was a growing trade in children, babies were stolen from their mothers, mothers were given money to separate from their children, mothers were deceived into believing that their children would have a good start in life and then return to their own family - the rapporteur. - mr president, the maastricht and amsterdam treaties both highlight measures to protect the environment. the commission's communication aims to take these considerations further into account in the energy sector. three objectives have been set: first, to promote energy efficiency; the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of the cost-effective. thirdly, the implementation of these objectives must be flexible to take account of rapidly changing markets and technologies. global warming is a major environmental problem, but it is obvious that it is not the only one we are facing. the energy and transport sectors are among the main contributors to emissions responsible for global warming. europe must do its part and set an example for the rest of the world, while recognizing that the greatest pressures on energy consumption will be exerted in the future by countries like the united states, which are rather lavish in their energy consumption, and by developing countries which, given their growing economies and living standards, will seek to increase their energy consumption, probably from polluting sources. the report therefore calls on the commission to promote best practice, encourage exchanges of views and experience and raise public awareness, while respecting the principle of subsidiarity. it must be acknowledged that energy policy is still to a large extent determined at the level of the member states. however, there is no doubt that energy efficiency is a topic that affects us all. the report also calls on the commission to support the process of mainstreaming these objectives into energy policy through research into the impact of climate change, research into all possible technologies, research into identifying the best indicators to measure the contribution to emission reductions and regular reporting to parliament. as regards possible legislative measures, the report calls on the commission to consider adapting existing legislation or introducing new measures that will reinforce these objectives. it also called on the commission to monitor and study the effects of all competitors, as well as developing countries, with a view to improving global environmental protection measures and significantly reducing emissions. the commission has omitted from its report a major aspect, namely nuclear energy. whatever your view of this energy and electricity source, it is a fact that it provides a significant share of europe's electricity without producing co2 or other greenhouse gases. that is why - and only because - this energy source was mentioned in the report. it would be unfortunate if this reference to nuclear energy diverted attention from the main objective of this report which is to improve energy efficiency, increase the supply from renewable energy sources and integrate our environmental objectives into our energy policy. it's a good start, and there's still a lot of work to be done.

in writing. - i respect the reasons why the representatives of the british delegation abstained on amendments nos 5 and 8 - concerning doctors in training - but i did not follow that line of action for the following reasons: firstly, it is a negotiable position and secondly, members of my family have been confronted with an extremely anxious and overworked nhs midwife, which prevents me from imposing on key medical staff longer working hours than are absolutely necessary.
in writing. -en) perhaps i should start by stating the historical and not circumstantial reason why i voted in favour of amendment no 5, article 1 (6) on doctors in training. my husband, dr. rhys jenkins, who is now a part-time general practitioner, once worked as much as 100 hours a week as a medical trainee. this firsthand knowledge of the problem made me aware of the dangers of forcing doctors to work such long hours. it puts patients' lives at risk and it can certainly have a negative effect on doctors' health. i believe that such a long and widespread transitional period as the council of ministers has proposed is unnecessary and inappropriate. in addition, there is a particularly acute problem in wales, where the medical association has estimated that 30% of doctors in training work more than the recommended 40 hours per week. in comparison, the estimated figure in scotland is as high as 10%. the profession is facing huge recruitment problems and a hemorrhage of doctors who travel to other countries because of excessive working hours.
in writing. - the members of the european parliamentary labour party abstained on amendments nos 5, 7 and 8 to the smet report on the working time directive. although the eplp members are committed to extending the scope of the working time directive, they understand the need to operate in a rational manner. we are committed to reducing the number of hours of work performed by trainee doctors but it is essential that this be done in a planned and structured way that does not jeopardise the care provided to patients. this directive will require an appropriate transitional period with progressive reductions in working time. flexibility was required for the fishing industry. this amendment does not recognise the reality of the requirements of the fishing industry and will have adverse effects on it.
in writing. - finally, we are filling a gap which dates back to 1993, when the working time directive was adopted. this legislation was a certain advance, but at the same time it excluded six million workers from its scope. these included personnel working in the transport sector, but also those working at sea (in particular offshore and 'doctors in training'). the exclusion of those workers was no longer tolerable in so far as the nature of their work did not differ from that of the workers covered by the provisions of the directive. the proposal we are discussing today therefore has a corrective purpose. the discussions were heated, particularly on the question of the offshore sector and doctors in training. in the latter area, the european commission's initial proposal proposed that doctors in training be brought within the scope of the directive through a seven-year transitional period. we have demanded that this be reduced to four years, with an intermediate limit of fifty-four hours per week (negotiable). this is the minimum that can be demanded if the nature of the profession is taken into account. it is the well-being of these doctors at work, the safety and health of their patients that are at stake! that is why we cannot accept the council's common position on this point, which calls for a transitional period of nine years! as for offshore workers, we have demanded that working hours can only be expressed in terms of an annual figure under collective agreements or agreements between the social partners. this provision will have to be reconsidered in the light of workers' health and safety within five years of the entry into force of the directive. the organisation of working time and the better reconciliation of work and private life it allows must benefit the greatest number of people. this is the condition for starting to talk about social europe. it's about time.

commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, agenda 2000 and numerous opinions of the european council, the european parliament and other european bodies have repeatedly stressed that in order to join the european union, the candidate countries of central and eastern europe must ensure high safety standards in their nuclear installations. i repeat what i have said on several occasions: the commission is not prepared to make any compromises on the question of nuclear safety. the european union has left no doubt that nuclear reactors which were considered impossible to modernise because of fundamental design flaws will have to be shut down in preparation for accession. the commission has also decided to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of radioactive waste. over the years, the european union has provided considerable assistance under the phare programme. since 1991, the commission has financed, to the tune of almost eur 2 million, concrete actions aimed at rapidly improving safety. however, it also made many efforts to close down the reactors that could not be upgraded. it is in this political context that i would like to place the rest of my statements and first of all to inform you that two of the three countries concerned have made commitments to shut down the reactors. they've set concrete deadlines for this shutdown. negotiations are under way with the third country and i am hopeful that we will reach a solution before the european council in helsinki. in early september, the lithuanian government adopted a new national energy strategy which reiterates the commitment to close unit 1 by 2005 and to set the date for the closure of unit 2 as part of the next national energy strategy to be adopted in 2004. the commission assumes that block 2 will be closed by 2009 at the latest. on 5 october, the new energy strategy was adopted by the lithuanian parliament by a clear majority of 63 votes to 31. on 28 september, the slovak government officially informed the commission of its decision to move the date of closure of reactors 1 and 2 of the bohunice v 1 plant to 2006 and 2008. this decision was taken after slovakia invested more than eur 200 million in improving nuclear safety in recent years. i know some of your expectations about bohunice's closure seem to have been dashed. i take those concerns seriously. an earlier shutdown of the reactors would have been desirable. i must add, however, that the closure of nuclear reactors is not feasible anywhere overnight. it must also be clear that the country in question needs enormous technical and financial support. i should also like to stress that the community acquis in the field of nuclear safety, and in particular radiation protection, is very limited. at present, each member state and therefore each candidate country is free to choose its own form of energy production. the only principle to which all the members of the union must adhere is to ensure that the highest internationally recognised safety standards are met. the commission therefore considers that the decisions taken by lithuania and slovakia to close reactors in the field of nuclear safety constitute the necessary commitments to justify the opening of accession negotiations with them. this does not exclude the possibility of greater flexibility. the commission considers that the lithuanian and slovak promises are essential steps towards effective closure, but the objective itself has not yet been achieved. we are now focusing on the practical implementation of the closure decision. lithuania will have to adopt a law on this closure formally instructing operators to initiate the closure procedure. an action plan for the implementation of the national energy strategy is being drawn up. slovakia will also have to start planning for the closure. our cooperation with these countries will therefore move to the implementation phase. the commission has committed itself to providing financial aid - in the form of non-repayable grants under the phare programme for 1999 - for the closure of the two nuclear power stations in lithuania and slovakia. the main part of these grants will be paid through an international fund administered by the ebrd. from the year 2000 onwards, we plan to provide an annual grant of eur 20 million for each reactor closure. the commission notes that the aid is not intended to cover the costs of the closure of the plant, but rather to support the follow-up measures in the conventional energy sector. in lithuania, for example, the liberalisation and modernisation of the non-nuclear electricity sector is proposed to compensate for the closure of the ignalina nuclear power station. in its conclusions on the regular reports published on 13 october, the commission stated that it favoured the opening of accession negotiations with bulgaria in 2000. we recommend, however, that they be submitted to a decision by the bulgarian government before the end of 1999 on an acceptable date for the closure of units 1 to 4 of the kozloduy nuclear power plant and on significant progress in the process of economic reform. i would like to stress that the decision to close kozloduy is a decisive condition. it will be difficult to reach a consensus on the opening of negotiations with bulgaria in helsinki if this problem is not resolved. i am currently in close contact with the bulgarian government on this matter. there are signs of political will to reach an acceptable solution since the bulgarian government has accepted the possibility of deviating from the closure deadlines set out in the country's energy strategy. however, no significant progress has been made in the negotiations so far. as in the case of lithuania and the slovak republic, the commission is ready to assist bulgaria by providing similar facilities as soon as sofia has decided to close the dangerous reactors. the commission is also prepared to grant euratom loans for the modernisation and refurbishment of units 5 and 6 of the kozloduy power station. the granting of this loan is conditional on an agreement on a date for closure of the four former blocks. after this comprehensive report on recent developments in non-renewable nuclear reactors in the candidate countries, i would like to say a few words about the renewable and non-renewable reactors in the nis, the newly independent states. in the past week, the members of the phare management committee gave a favourable opinion on the commission's programme to release eur 11 million from phare resources to finance safety measures at nuclear power stations in the candidate countries and measures to be taken by the licensing authorities in the candidate countries. the commission intends to continue this support throughout the financial perspective for the period 2000-06. in parallel, the tacis programme will continue to provide financial assistance to beneficiaries to achieve the objectives of agenda 2000 and in particular to strengthen the safety culture, improve the management of spent nuclear material, work towards the halt and closure of chernobyl, the joint working group with armenia on the medzamor nuclear power plant and other measures. the commission knows - and i am sure the honourable members are of the same opinion - that the closure of nuclear power stations is a serious handicap for economies in transition and particularly for those countries which became independent states shortly after their separation from the soviet union. the commission considers it its duty to achieve this objective as quickly as possible. but we cannot do it all by ourselves. the international community must act together. it has an interest in the establishment of european safety standards. the member states and the international community will also have to offer assistance and advice to the candidate countries. the increase in safety standards for nuclear power plants, whether through renovation or the closure of reactors deemed unsuitable for modernisation, will continue to entail significant costs. the commission would therefore like to organise, together with the applicant countries, donor conferences with a view to setting up special funds for lithuania, slovakia and bulgaria. the first of these conferences, for lithuania, is expected to be held in early 2000. we urge member states and third countries, and in particular those with a regional interest in northern, central and southern europe, to contribute to these three funds. we will plan these funds carefully and will ensure in particular that the chernobyl reactor decommissioning fund, supported by the g7, will receive additional resources next year. we have achieved some results, but we still have a lot of work to do in the future. we must insist that nuclear security be given the highest priority at the eastern borders of the union. we now have a realistic prospect of the actual closure of the problematic nuclear reactors in the applicant countries. this is an economic and political duty. the european parliament can be sure that the commission will take up this task with the greatest urgency. i hope that the commission can count on your support in carrying out this difficult task, which is in the interests of our citizens. negotiations, that nothing will be done without the european parliament and that the wishes of the european parliament in this matter are therefore of great importance. i would like to make it clear that we are focusing on reactors which the g7 expertise - in 1992, if i remember correctly - has judged to be unmodernisable, not because of safety deficiencies in their operation but because of their design. these are reactors which are neither safe by design nor can be upgraded, at least at reasonable cost. in all these cases, there is only one reasonable solution to the problem: closure, and certainly as soon as possible. anyone who considers these reactors to be a safety risk, and we believe that, should seek their closure, and the sooner the better. the only difficulty is that the negotiations on the acquis communautaire, the accession negotiations, provide us with nothing more than a means of political pressure. as i have already said, the european union has very limited powers in this area. so we are exerting political pressure, which means that what comes out of it will be a political solution. in order to achieve this political solution, it is not enough to consider what we want - i am fully aware that this is a very topical issue in some member states, and particularly in austria, as the debate has shown - but it is also necessary to consider that in the applicant countries this issue has in some way acquired a practically theological significance. in bulgaria, for example, i can tell you that the closure of kozloduy has been the number one issue for months, the issue that inflames all national antagonisms. in this context and in view of the balance of power in the country and the fact that the acceptance of the closure of kozloduy will be used against the government in the next elections - as will also be the case in lithuania and slovakia - i must really say that the steps taken by the bulgarian government so far have been courageous decisions. we cannot avoid finding a middle way, that is, setting a date that we could accept in an extreme case. in each case, this date must be clearly separated from the reactor's expected operating life. we have succeeded in this with ignalina and bohunice. i would like to say one more thing about bohunice, because for some time now people have been trying to drag me into this austrian debate. we will not succeed because i fully agree with the austrian position that we should try to achieve better results. wolfgang schüssel and i made this clear to the council yesterday. the austrian foreign minister raised this issue yesterday in the council. i said that i supported his position and that i fully supported all efforts to take full advantage of the available room for manoeuvre. the problem, as you are well aware, madam president, is that when i took office i was confronted with an agreement with slovakia. he was ready, he was committed. unfortunately, it was not made public until a few days after i took office. i could hardly criticize what the commission had negotiated with slovakia. it was impossible to react any differently than i did. but from the outset and on several occasions in this parliament, i have said that in the case of bohunice i believe that more discussion is needed and that the slovak government is suggesting that more could be achieved. some colleagues have raised the question of whether it is really sensible to invest in the safety of plants that we want to shut down. it is indeed a highly complex issue and, in my view, almost a matter of conscience. in recent years the commission has also made financial investments to ensure the safety of the plants we are discussing until they are shut down. the main focus of the actions was on improving the safety culture of these countries, establishing independent safety inspection authorities and training those responsible for carrying out these inspections. we have not financed any investment that would have extended the life of these plants in any way. there's no way that's going to happen. unfortunately, we also have to distinguish between the soviet-designed nuclear power stations in the candidate countries, which i have mentioned, and their counterparts outside the candidate countries. the leverage we have is very different. in the first case, the political leverage is very strong because these countries want to join the eu and we very clearly subject this membership to a solution to this problem that we consider to be defensible. in the case of russia, belarus, armenia, ukraine and other countries, we naturally do not have such a powerful lever. i am, however, firmly convinced that the european union must also work to raise safety standards in these countries. in fact, it's a terrible dilemma. we know that a nuclear power plant really needs to be shut down. however, we are faced with a political situation which makes this decision impossible. the question then is: are you doing anything to at least guarantee the safety or even improve the safety of the plant, knowing full well that this could lead to the plant you want to close being operated for longer than it would otherwise be? i must say that these are questions that can only disturb our sleep. our colleague was quite right. but when it comes to nuclear safety, i think that we cannot ignore any measures which might improve the current level of safety in any way. when we are faced with plants which we want to close but cannot close for the political reasons i have mentioned, i see no other option than to do what is necessary to at least eliminate the most glaring deficiencies, however difficult and complicated that may be. so that is my answer to the very fundamental question that has been asked in this chamber. we shall certainly be returning to this subject more often. i hope very much - and i am not saying this without reason - that the next time we discuss this matter i shall be able to report a situation which is clearly better than the present situation. aspect of the european political integration process. the danger is that pressure will be put on the union to become the first organization to be called upon when the next crisis arises, with nato gradually relegated to the only remaining role of collective defence organization. nato's transatlantic dynamism and solidarity can only be preserved if it remains closely and continuously engaged in day-to-day crisis management. of course, since the europeans are not proposing additional forces, the capacity for autonomous action of the european union is mainly a matter of political decisions. well-established structures of nato, not an institutional geometry of european staffs. the aim is more effective security to which europeans and north americans each contribute in greater proportions. we must not recruit our armies under the pretext of political integration by putting them in a different uniform.

this requires a multilateral system that is fair, transparent, accountable and that links trade and development. it should take into account the impact of liberalisation on investment, competition rules, abusive subsidies, inadequate labour standards, environmental protection, intellectual property rights, trade facilitation, public procurement, improved access to agricultural markets, improved access to commercial markets including services, consumer protection and capacity development. the european union is unique in its history of relations with countries around the world. i am thinking of britain with the commonwealth and france with the french-speaking countries. we can send a clear message to seattle that this is a sign of the contribution that this house and its members can make to world trade.

- i would like to say first of all how much i welcome the resolution of this parliament. it will be a clear sign to the world of the seriousness with which we are dealing with the question of the year 2000 and will, we hope, be an example for others to follow. but time is clearly running out. this means that despite all the good intentions at present, the risks of failure are inevitable. the high level of interconnections between countries, particularly in the western world, makes it impossible to predict exactly where and when such outages will occur. the level of unpredictability is higher the higher the level of integration. the situation in eastern europe is also far from reassuring. the lack of information from this region was still a concern to the commission last june, and the situation is becoming more worrying as we move eastwards. the safest approach is to shut down all these plants for the millennium, but how could lithuania deprive itself of 75% of its ignalina production capacity? by leaving people in the dark and without water? the west must offer its help, and i therefore welcome this resolution which calls on the oecd countries to provide the necessary resources to do so. i will end very quickly with an anecdote that would be amusing if the situation were not so serious. the americans and the russians have recently put up red telephones so that they can communicate in case of problems related to the year 2000 bug and, in all but one case, they have discovered problems related to the year 2000 bug on these lines! nothing will be guaranteed in the weeks to come; we must act now to reduce risks around the world and i welcome the contribution to this process that our resolution makes.
commission. - mr president, i shall answer your questions and your comments on matters which are within the commission's competence. the way we see the situation in the member states, in the nuclear candidate countries and in the newly independent states is as follows. let me first point out that in fact, few nuclear power stations, even in the most developed countries, use computer software as a vital part of their safety system. our member states with nuclear power stations have been working on this issue for at least two years, and the information we have indicates that the remedial measures are now practically complete, as is all the work on emergency planning. the commission has encouraged the exchange of knowledge and good practice in this case, but we have not seen the need to intervene more in our activities with the member states. the same is not true of some countries in central and eastern europe and some newly independent states, whose response to the problem has been slower. some people only started to pay attention to this issue at the end of 1998. these countries were supported in their work by the international atomic energy agency, which revised their analyses of the scale of the problem for a significant number of plants; mrs plooij-van gorsel referred to the work done so far and here is my answer, madam president: the work of the agency and the countries operating these plants has not revealed any bug problem on the systems essential for safety. the commission has provided additional aid to certain nuclear power plant operators. we have financed missions of eu experts to three plants in russia and to three plants in ukraine. in addition, we have offered our support to nuclear regulators since the beginning of this year, and we are now supporting such projects in bulgaria, slovakia and russia. while no safety critical system elements are affected, a number of other systems, including those informing the operator, could be affected and their failure could indirectly threaten nuclear safety by overloading operators, as has been indicated. on the basis of the information available to us, we believe that the countries of central and eastern europe have generally made good progress in correcting these systems. comparatively, the newly independent states of the former soviet union are undoubtedly moving more slowly in their healing efforts, but all of them say that the work will be completed by the end of this year. we support these clean-up efforts by contributing to the activities of two international scientific and technical centres, the one in moscow and the one in kiev, and if necessary we are prepared to provide additional support for these programmes, given that, as you said in the debate, we are now very close to the year 2000 and the main thing was to start dealing with this in good time. here is both my answer and our contribution to the solution of this important problem.

in writing. - the convention on the rights of the child is the most productive of the international conventions: all countries in the world, except somalia and the usa, have signed it. the objectives of the convention reflect an unprecedented international response: measures to be implemented in international law to protect the rights of the world's most innocent and vulnerable citizens. the draft resolution we voted on today aims to ensure that the elements protected by this convention are protected in other legal bases and frameworks. we seek to echo the expectations of citizens who cannot speak out, and to protect those who cannot protect themselves. children should be protected by those who have their best interests at heart. we must therefore emphasize the role of the family, and especially of the parents, in protecting children. in its efforts to create a legal basis for the protection and treatment of children, the state must bow to the primacy of the right of parents to protect and their children. we must ensure that the family has, and i quote from the convention on the rights of the child, "the protection and assurance it needs to be able to play its full role in the community".

the next item is the continuation of the debate on the report (a5-0063/1999) by mrs giannakou-koutsikou, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on a european union action plan to combat drugs (2000-2004) (com (1999) 239).
- few subjects are more striking in their cultural approach to the eu than the one in the netherlands. i think this report reflects a good consensus and i congratulate mrs giannakou-koutsikou on her work in drawing up this report. i am one of a growing minority in the group of the european liberal, democratic and reformist party and also in this house who believe that a radical change in our approach is necessary. why would you do that ? aside from the ethical weakness of the prohibitionist argument (the state has no right to prevent a responsible adult from using drugs), the fact is that prohibition does not work. our approach, based on controlling the supply of drugs, requires enormous resources. according to the police in bristol, my constituency, 85% of crime is drug-related. it is destroying our urban centres, which are a huge market for drug traffickers, who sometimes even become role models for disillusioned young people. it fills our prisons with people who need care more than imprisonment and it creates disproportionate discrimination against ethnic minorities, some of whom have a culture that is less critical of drug use than others. more importantly, it helps to finance other forms of criminal activity and to strengthen international organized crime. we must at least consider redirecting resources from the fight against drug supply to the fight against demand. - mr president, i congratulate my colleague on her report. in my region of europe, 3 million people use illegal drugs, 28% of whom are aged 16 to 29 and 14% are aged 14 to 15. there are 12,000 new cases of drug addiction every year, 70,000 drug-related crimes every year and 1,200 drug-related deaths every year. we may not be winning this battle, but we must not lose it. we need a multi-pronged policy, we need to act together to stop the producers, traffickers and dealers, but we also need education and health policies; finally, we must encourage research. if we just suppress supply, not demand, the street price of drugs will go up and people will commit more crime to pay for it. many of the amendments to this report are therefore relevant. we have to educate the young. we need role models from the world of music, fashion and film to get the message across to young people: not just by saying "no", it doesn't work, but by telling them the truth. the truth is that drugs can be pleasurable, but they can also be harmful to health. it can cause cancer, cardiovascular disease, memory and concentration problems, testicular problems, and more. this too young people must understand. using drugs is wrong, but we must help those who are willing to accept our help. i will never forget, when i was minister for the fight against drugs, my meeting with a young man who had lost his health, his friends, his relations, his family, his job, his future and his self-respect. we were helping him out of the black hole of addiction. i stupidly asked him, "do you feel like you've won the battle?" he said, "i have a lifetime of struggle ahead of me, and if i ever think i've won, i'm lost". he deserves our support. he needs research so that we can provide him with effective treatment and we need to give him that support and that trust. but it would be so much better if we could destroy this scourge by persuading the young people of future generations that drugs are simply not for them, that they are not worth the risk.
the rapporteur. - (en) this report calls for no dispute or controversy except on one point which concerns all those who are listening to me. the proposal aims to develop a computerised image archiving system to help detect forged travel documents. i guess we all agree it's worth it. what, then, is the only point of contention? the question is whether this decision will be taken behind closed doors in brussels by officials and ministers or whether parliament will have a right of access. the 15 national parliaments cannot have it because it is a european proposal and that task will therefore fall to us or to no one. the background to this proposal is that in january this year the commission put forward the same proposal, stating that its objective was to detect the documents used by illegal immigrants. the proposal was abandoned when the treaty of amsterdam came into force in may. it has now been reintroduced by the german government, as a national government is entitled to do under the treaty of amsterdam. the problem, however, is that the german government declares that its objective is to combat, i quote, 'crime', without mentioning the word immigration. why would you do that ? because in the amsterdam treaty, immigration issues are transferred from the third pillar to the first pillar and become for the first time the responsibility of parliament. however, criminal matters remain within the third pillar, in which we have no right of review and no responsibility whatsoever. i therefore conclude that the german government is trying to avoid parliament's right of scrutiny in its proposal. the committee didn't like it. the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs has invited the finnish presidency and the german government to come and answer our questions on this proposal. the finnish presidency replied by letter to the committee that it would not be coming to answer our questions, but that we could still put questions in plenary. well, this is a plenary session. where is the council of ministers? everyone can see that the chairs are empty except for a lovely lady in grey who is a civil servant and is not allowed to speak. i hope, however, that she will convey this message. i regret to say that the fact that the german government has sought to evade parliament's right of scrutiny by keeping this under the third pillar and that the finnish presidency has not even appeared to answer our questions, either in committee or in plenary, seriously tarnishes the reputation of the finns, who have hitherto enjoyed a superb reputation for openness and democracy. i also regret that they are not here to answer my accusations. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. i ask everyone here to vote tomorrow to support the committee in establishing parliamentary scrutiny of this new policy element which is part of our powers under the amsterdam treaty. - mr president, i would also like to support the main points of the german council initiative to improve the exchange of information on forged travel documents and to strengthen border security in the european union both for member states such as my own, the united kingdom, which are not part of schengen, and for those on the perimeter of the union. my country, the united kingdom, has recently seen a huge increase in the number of people entering its territory, and in my previous job, as a doctor at london's central hospital, i witnessed a significant degree of illegal immigration and fraudulent abuse of our generous asylum system. the uk receives about 7,000 new asylum applications a month, of which 80% are found to be fictitious after investigation. that is about 100,000 people a year, including their families coming into my country. i have personally seen a nigerian asylum seeker granted asylum on the basis of a false liberian passport, an albanian family posing as kosovars, another nigerian who had lent his british passport to his cousin who was able to enter the uk posing as him and then commit a crime, and an algerian who was living under the identity of a french citizen and had bought his identity card on the paris black market. these are just a few examples of the many abuses i have witnessed firsthand, and we know that the immigration authorities are faced with these abuses every day. how can we hope that our own immigration authorities and our own police forces will be able to crack down on the systematic abuse of the system? it is our duty to remember that this constant influx of illegal immigrants is weighing particularly heavily on our urban centres, our national health service, our social services and our social security system while putting our limited housing resources under enormous pressure. unfortunately, it seems that many of these asylum seekers were led through continental europe into the belief that they were heading for one of our channel ports knowing that we had a permissive asylum policy that instantly granted the right to housing and social security. the british conservative party is in principle formally opposed to the transfer to the first pillar, under article 63 of the amsterdam treaty, of visa, immigration and asylum policies, and i must therefore express my disagreement with the rapporteur on this point. we are nevertheless in favour of intergovernmental cooperation under the third pillar through joint action by the council for the exchange of such information, including that relating to falsified travel documents, in order to combat crime and in particular international crime which does not respect national borders. organized crime seems to have found an easy and lucrative business in the illegal trafficking of people, often willing to sacrifice their life savings to enter wealthy western countries in the hope of starting a new life. so i think this initiative is a step in the right direction because it uses modern computer technology to digitize images to help law enforcement and interior ministries to cooperate across the union. i think this is a good example of the kind of project that my party in the united kingdom can support as long as it is carried out on a flexible intergovernmental basis.

diversifying information on the council's action and priorities. the aim is to lay the foundations for a more in-depth and analytical debate on the european union's action in favour of human rights. i would also like to take this opportunity to mention the first european union forum on human rights, which ended today before this session, and in which many of us also participated. the forum was the venue for an active and forward-looking debate on many of the themes covered in the annual report. this forum was intended to be the commitment to a more sustained and wider dialogue on the priorities and challenges of the european union's human rights policy. this approach was also supported by the participants. i myself am convinced that the forum will not be left without a follow-up. all comments on how to develop and make this forum more effective are naturally welcome. but why is it in the european union's interest to publish a human rights report every year? firstly, the council considers that this can enhance the transparency of the european union's human rights policy. as you know, promoting transparency is one of the priority areas of the finnish presidency. transparency is of particular importance in the area of human rights. it is essential to strengthen dialogue and cooperation, because we all have our own role to play in this regard. the annual report covers the period from the beginning of june 1998 to the end of june 1999. this period has been chosen so that the results of the june european summits can be included in the report. it is planned to adopt the same division in future reports. secondly, this report aims to increase the coherence of the european union's human rights policy. i personally believe that the key challenge for the european union's human rights policy is precisely coherent and credible action in the various fora. the annual report provides for the first time a synthesis of the european union's overall action in the various international organisations and our relations with third countries. the annual report examines action in the field of the first and second pillars. in compiling the report, we noticed that nowhere else had this information been collected before. we also learned that there was real scope for strengthening the coherence of the european union's action beyond the limits of the pillars. the annual report focuses this time on the european union's external relations. this first annual report nevertheless includes a section on the european union's action to prevent racism on its own territory. the credibility of the european union's action implies that we ourselves observe the same human rights principles as those we demand of others. in the future, the internal situation of the european union will have to be considered more broadly, as was noted during the preparation of the annual report. the necessary capacities will have to be developed. for example, asylum and refugee issues could be given more consideration in the future, as they do have a crucial 'human rights' dimension. the purpose of the annual report is to present the european union's activity and the thematic aspects for the period chosen. it is therefore not intended to be an exhaustive description of the human rights situation in the various countries. it is not impossible that the need may arise in the future. it may be necessary to examine the situation in the individual countries more closely. however, this would require more developed monitoring and analysis mechanisms and capabilities than at present. the first chapters of the annual report set out the principles of the european union's human rights policy. these principles include universality and indivisibility. secondly, we have tried to present the main actors and systems in the field of community action and in international organisations. priorities and thematic human rights issues were also discussed, such as women's rights, children's rights and minority rights, as well as the fight against the death penalty and racism. the importance of economic, social and cultural rights is also rightly emphasised. i know very well that the content and form of the annual report are still subject to improvement. but we have tried to make it concise and easy to read. as soon as the report was adopted by the council, it was also made available on the internet. it will also be published in all the languages of the european union in the council's series of publications and will be widely disseminated. this is because we believe that an important part of human rights work is to make people aware of what human rights mean. the treaty of amsterdam and the human rights regulations which have just entered into force improve the possibilities for action by the european union in promoting human rights. these increased possibilities must now be given concrete and relevant content. in this respect, the european union's human rights policy is in a dynamic development phase. the reactions, including those of the european parliament, to this first annual report and the proposals it contains are very welcome. this would enable us to make progress in the next report on the common path we have chosen. there is one point i would like to mention separately. as i said at the beginning, deeper and more analytical cooperation with other european organizations, such as the council of europe and the osce, is needed. this is not just a polite wish, but an extremely important priority which the european union must take into account when considering its action in this area. redundant actions will have to be avoided. we are not in favour of creating double standards, which would cause problems not only for the applicant countries but also for ourselves. monitoring human rights means in practice monitoring the application of these standards. it is precisely the development of these standards that is the area in which the council of europe has the most experience. our union should therefore benefit from the experience of others. i believe that the group set up to draw up the charter of fundamental rights also plays a very important role. the composition of the group shall endeavour to take account of this different competence. i hope that we will receive good advice on how to improve the european union's action to promote human rights, so that we can really add value and not just rename problems by another name. my vision for the future is that human rights will play an increasingly important role in very different contexts. the active debate on human rights at the wto round of negotiations in seattle is a good example of this. the results of the tampere summit are also worth mentioning. in the future, the european union will have to take more clearly into account the effect of any action it takes on the realisation of human rights. the european parliament - you, ladies and gentlemen - has a very important role to play in this respect. i appreciate the fact that the european parliament closely follows human rights issues and comments, sometimes strongly or even sharply, on government actions. the european parliament thus significantly complements cooperation between governments. i hope that the first annual report on human rights will reinforce this development, which we can only welcome. - mr president, commissioner lamy and others have spoken of the seattle meeting in terms of failure. i still believe, however, that if the eu and america in particular were to learn the lessons of the past few weeks, the seattle meeting could still go down in history not as a failure but as the moment when world leaders finally realised that they had to take a radically different approach to international trade. they must first understand that the rich countries cannot continue to receive everything for nothing. if they are right to link environmental and social problems with trade problems, they will have to prove that they are not motivated by protectionism and in return they will have to guarantee substantial benefits to the developing countries. these benefits could include free access for all products from the poorest countries, the abolition of maximum tariffs and agreements to stop export dumping. secondly, it is clear that trade matters can no longer be kept secret by the most powerful members of the wto. the developing countries are showing a new determination to oppose this marginalization. the playing field between rich and poor countries is anything but fair. if we take only negotiating capacity, the eu and america were present in seattle with a whole army of lawyers and advisers. poor countries had very little. i have also heard - and i would be glad to know whether this is true or not - that 30 wto members could not even afford to be present at the seattle negotiations. the wto process must be made more democratic and transparent. i believe that a forum is needed to discuss proposals for radical reforms with the environment and development groups who have been working on this subject for many years. we don't have to reinvent the wheel. good proposals have been put forward. we must learn from them. finally, wto members must finally listen to the 1,200 non-governmental organizations from nearly 100 different countries. these ngos signed a declaration calling for no further trade liberalisation until the social and environmental impacts of the current liberalisation have been examined and problems clearly identified. the impasse in the seattle talks gives us an opportunity to do just that.

commission -(en) the cologne european council decided that a charter of fundamental rights of the european union should be drawn up before the european council in december 2000. it has decided that this charter should be drawn up by a body composed of 15 representatives of the heads of state or government, 16 members of the european parliament, including the author of the question, 30 members of the national parliaments and myself, representing the president of the commission. the composition of this body was finally decided in tampere and its first meeting is to take place next friday, 17 december. the nature of this charter is a very fundamental question which the council has nevertheless preferred to leave open. on the basis of the conclusions, it will be necessary to consider whether the charter should be incorporated into the treaties and, if so, how. although the final decision on the status of the charter is left to the heads of state or government, the body responsible for drawing up the charter will have to consider in its proposal either a legally binding text ready to be incorporated into the treaties or a solemn political declaration. these discussions will also have to be conducted with due regard to the close links with the preparatory work of the igc. the commission is of the opinion that the european charter of fundamental rights must address two very different concerns: visibility and legal certainty. as regards visibility, it is reasonable to assume that a solemn political declaration issued by the european institutions and relayed through all communication channels would be sufficient. as regards legal certainty, however, we must look at how the european charter of fundamental rights can help to improve the level of protection of these rights within the european union and, in this context, it is hard to imagine that a non-binding text can help to clarify and transcend the current system of protection. the commission believes that the charter to be presented by the heads of state or government must have real added value and that the best way to achieve this is to focus on the fundamental rights which result from the union itself. the body responsible for drawing up the charter will have to develop a text which has real political significance and can be incorporated into the treaty. it is clear that the principle of drawing up such a charter is generally welcomed and that citizens hope that it will serve as a reference text in this field. the commission is convinced that they must not be disappointed.

commission i am aware of price differences between the united kingdom and other member states and i share the honourable member's concerns. the commission found that these differences were partly due to the strength of the pound sterling, while member states which tax motor vehicles heavily have low net prices. this is particularly the case in denmark, finland and the netherlands. i think that greater price transparency and the introduction of the euro are increasingly encouraging customers in member states with high market prices to buy their vehicles in other member states. this parallel trade is an important factor in the convergence of prices throughout the union and is directly linked to the market. the commission has taken several initiatives to guarantee this freedom for consumers. in its report on the application of regulation 1475/95 on car distribution, due before the end of 2000, the commission will assess the impact of the tax-free distribution system on vehicle prices. in fact, this report should form the basis for future discussions on the future legal framework to be given to the automotive distribution sector after the expiry of the current regulation on 30 september 2002.

mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. i believe that the defence of consumer interests is the centrepiece of the european union's competition policy. would we go so far as to say that a single market is truly a single market when there is unity of price? i do not think so because there will always be factors which justify certain price differences. it could also be considered that a perfect unity of prices in a given market may conceal the presence of a dominant cartel in that market. however, i agree with you that many of the price differences in the single market today are due to the remaining disagreements and obstacles. two powerful factors are currently at work to help the market overcome these divergences and this will increasingly be the case. the first is, of course, the euro, which will make price comparisons easier, and the second, which has a major impact on the distribution of goods and services, is the internet. you ask whether the commission should not intervene in certain cases of wide price divergences. we should and we do. as regards the motor vehicle sector in particular, you should know that the commission has already taken several initiatives in the past and, even more recently, it has taken action against the restrictions imposed by car manufacturers on parallel imports of vehicles. the publication of comparative lists of car prices is another measure which goes much in the same direction. the last edition was published on 22 july 1999. we agree that the commission could also use the instruments at its disposal in the context of competition policy. let me tell you, that's what she does.
- i am pleased to note that the commissioner, with the british minister for trade and industry, mr byers, has succeeded in creating the impression that the european automobile industry is leading, if i may say so, the british consumers astray. but i must confess that i do not agree with you when you say that it is simply a matter of exchange rates, because that is not enough to explain why some vehicles cost about £4,000 more in the uk than, say, in the netherlands. if it were simply a matter of exchange rates, prices would also fall according to the whims of the exchange rate. why, for example, are imported cars - which now account for over 70% of the uk market - more expensive when the pound rises? how is it that the level of exports by british car manufacturers to the continent is reaching record levels when exports are precisely costing more? why are uk-built vehicles cheaper on the continent when the pound's price is driving up the price of our exports? i'm afraid i can't see the logic in all this. i think, after an 18-month investigation by a british newspaper in the wake of your own investigation, that time is running out and the car industry now wants to find a solution to the problem. if i were to bring together the representatives of industry, dealers and manufacturers, would you agree to join them in discussing ways of getting out of this situation, if necessary by resorting to the instruments of competition?
commission -en) i thank you, mrs mccarthy, also for your insistence on the urgency of using the competition instruments, which we are already doing. let me draw your attention once again to the fact that we have carried out quite a few investigations into restrictions on parallel imports and in some cases have already reached a conclusion leading to rather substantial fines. it would of course be inappropriate to attribute price differences, particularly for motor vehicles, to exchange rate differences alone. i have mentioned this as one factor, but it is understood that it is not the only one. the differences in the taxation of different categories of vehicles is a factor, of course, but it brings us to the question of taxation and the difficulty the eu has in making decisions in this area. i also appreciate your invitation to a round table. i shall be glad to consider it, taking into account all the invitations a commissioner may receive. as you are no doubt aware, we are preparing a report on the application of the existing block exemption regulation, which is currently attracting a good deal of our attention. we received many replies to the questionnaires we had sent out for consultation purposes. the report, which is due to be published at the end of the year, will not contain any proposals per se but will contain an analysis of the impact of the tax-free distribution system planned for the end of 2000 and a specific analysis of the impact of the block exemptions. it should serve as a basis for subsequent decisions.

- in the last decades of the 20th century, we have seen a series of food alerts. in many cases, legitimate concerns are overblown when the media are busy feeding panic, sometimes making the facts look good. there are probably not enough journalists with a good scientific knowledge, able to measure subjects such as risk. or, as i suspect, the sensational "some" that increase newspaper sales may be more important than consumer information, information that allows consumers to make their own decisions when they make their purchases. product labelling is an important way of countering this misinformation. it is true that it is possible to go too far and provide technical data which confuses rather than informs. when we look at the details of this directive and others, we will, i hope, bear in mind that a lady dragging her two or three irritable children to the supermarket will not have time to read a detailed label. it must be possible to obtain information at a glance on the origin, the method of production and other details in a simple and clear manner. today, food labels are at best vague; at worst, deliberately misleading. so you can be forgiven for thinking that bacon labelled 'uk-packaged' was produced in the uk according to our strictest health standards, which is not the case. a parmentier hash with the label 'product from the united kingdom' may well contain beef from botswana, zimbabwe or elsewhere in the world. that's not enough. labelling regulations should address these problems. i now turn to the intolerable situation we are currently facing with regard to the extension of the voluntary labelling scheme for beef. what would the union do if it were a company and not a country that chose to ignore the legislation that other companies apply? - oral question b5-0038/99 by mrs rothley and others, on book prices in germany and austria.
- mr president, my country, the united kingdom, has had a long political debate on the value of an agreement imposing the resale price of books. the debate ended with the abolition of the agreement on the price of books. there is no evidence in the uk that the abolition of the agreement has resulted in a reduction in choice, an increase in prices or a decline in the number of specialist bookshops. on the contrary, the number of books sold and of publishing houses seems to be increasing. that's a very good thing. i think that's my belief, because i think books are meant to be read. at least that's the conclusion i came to when i studied english literature at university. under the principle of subsidiarity, any member state is free to impose a fixed resale price on books if it so wishes. similarly, if two or more member states wish to create an internal fixed resale price area, they should do so. but they must not lose sight of compatibility with the rules of the single market. such a regulatory system cannot influence the price of books sold outside the jurisdiction of the member state concerned. nor can he influence the books brought or re-introduced into his territory. this new sales channel, which is developing alongside e-commerce, is becoming more widespread and popular. it fully respects the principles of the single market and offers enormous opportunities for small specialised businesses. the idea of imposing a fixed resale price is intolerant and runs counter to the principles of the single market. i even equate it with a concrete form of censorship and an artificial rationing of the supply of books in favour of the more privileged. i believe that this is also detrimental to the legitimate and lawful trade in the community and threatens to level down literary trade in europe, to relegate literature to the level of pornographic magazines distributed - if my information is correct - in letter boxes in unmarked kraft paper envelopes and to reduce the legitimate trade in books in the free world to the fraudulent introduction and passage of so-called corrupt literature from eastern europe. one thing is certain, i am against this principle, because i think it is old-fashioned, intolerant, reactionary and, in the long run, philistine.
commission. - (it) mr president, i thank all the participants in this debate, which i found politically and culturally interesting. i would like to assure the participants in the debate that the commission and i share their interest in culture and the book, that we recognize the cultural importance of the book and that we are prepared to take account of these specific features. mr karas recalled that i had already stated that i wanted competition policy to be included in the soziale marktwirtschaft (social market economy). i confirm this and ask you all not to regard competition as something abstract and harmful to citizens. competition is the citizen's main ally. the essential purpose of competition is to safeguard the interests of consumers in terms of price and quality and to protect small and mediumsized enterprises against the excesses of large enterprises. i am therefore prepared to acknowledge the importance of culture, but i would ask you not to fall into the intellectual trap of thinking that competition is not in the interests of citizens. the task of competition is to combat cartels, abuse of dominant positions and mergers, to create greater areas of economic freedom, but we know that economic freedom often goes hand in hand with civil freedom, as the past experience of countries where economic freedom did not exist shows. i therefore believe that it is possible to create a harmonious culture policy and a competition policy without raising artificial and sterile antagonisms.

commission. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this debate on human rights shows once again the need to remain vigilant in the face of these questions. all the cases we have discussed this afternoon are cases of fundamental violations of human rights. in the case of the death penalty in the united states and yemen, it is a matter of the fundamental right to life. in the case of discrimination against women in kuwait and afghanistan, it is the right to civic equality. in the case of djibouti, it is the right to freedom of opinion, to freedom of political action. in the case of nicaragua - on this point i have a different opinion from those who have spoken here - it is very clearly a question of the rule of law as such and the fact that in a rule of law one must be protected from arbitrary acts of the supreme power of the state. in view of the short time i have left, i would simply like to make a few further remarks on behalf of the commission. as regards the death penalty, we all agree that it is not compatible with our european standards. she must be condemned most severely. the execution of the death penalty is an inhuman act, which should have no place actually being introduced or carried out if possible. this also applies to the cases discussed here. the european union has set clear procedural rules for cases where the minimum standards are not yet - mr president, i do not intend to delay the work of the house unnecessarily. i do not want to get into a debate on the amendments, since this can be settled by a vote. one thing must be said, however. the process is not ideal, mrs doyle and other members are right, but the problem we have in the committee on transport and regional policy, which is the committee responsible, is that the council asked us for urgency at the last minute because someone, somewhere, realised that our house needed to pass a resolution in order for the fund in question to continue to operate. the only way to proceed was therefore to follow this very rapid procedure by letter from the president through the committee. we thought it was understood that there would be no amendments. unfortunately, that was not the case. it must be stressed, however, that given the time available to us, the commission and parliament worked as quickly and efficiently as possible in circumstances which proved difficult so that the money for this very important fund could be released next year.
in writing. - the amendments are inadmissible for the following reasons: the objectives of the fund do not include the promotion of large-scale inward investment. the fund exists to promote rural and urban development and community development, to develop skills and to improve the environment; the arguments put forward by the green amendments are fallacious. the fund does not play, nor could it have played, any role in the raytheon project. the amendments are simply to prevent the fund from doing something it could not do anyway. the proposed regulation aims to allow for the continuation of the eu financial contribution to the fund; the court of justice has held that the commission's intention to adopt the contested regulation is not to alter the substance of regulation (ec) no 2614/97, which was the reason for the adoption of the emergency procedure. as to substance, the projects cited in the greens' arguments are not military projects.
